course.title: The Roman Republic
course.description: From the end of the kings to Augustus, read through the people who wrote about it. Each lesson uses one stretch of Roman history to practise a skill from the History course: reading a source for its purpose, weighing a later account, separating cause from condition, and telling change from continuity.
course.audience: A curious adult who may have done the History course and wants a period to apply it to. They know that Rome had kings, a Republic and emperors, and may have heard of Hannibal and Caesar, but they have not read the ancient writers or asked who wrote each account and why.

paragraphs: From the end of the kings to Augustus, read through the people who wrote about it. Each lesson uses one stretch of Roman history to practise a skill from the History course: reading a source for its purpose, weighing a later account, separating cause from condition, and telling change from continuity.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what Livy, Polybius, Sallust, Caesar, Plutarch and Augustus each wrote for, and weigh what each can tell us.
You'll be able to tell a founding tradition from evidence for the events it describes.
You'll be able to say which body held which power under the Republic's constitution, and how the Struggle of the Orders changed it.
You'll be able to separate the conditions, causes and trigger of the Second Punic War, and read a casualty figure for who counted it.
You'll be able to compare two explanations of why the Republic broke down and say what each could see from where its writer stood.
You'll be able to put the main events from 509 BCE to 27 BCE in order and work out the intervals between them.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on History: How the Past Is Known.

modules.title: Founding and constitution
modules.description: What the Romans said about their beginnings, how a Greek observer described the Republic's offices, and how the first written laws came out of a quarrel between the orders.

modules.title: Italy and Carthage
modules.description: How Rome came to rule Italy, why it went to war with Carthage a second time, and what the accounts of Hannibal's victories can and cannot tell us.

modules.title: Empire and reform
modules.description: What conquest did to the city and the army, read through writers who disagree about why, with the Gracchi, Marius and Sulla as the cases.

modules.title: The end of the Republic
modules.description: Catiline, Cicero and the triumvirate, Caesar in his own words and in a later account, and Augustus telling his own story.

concepts.title: Tradition
concepts.summary: A story handed down about the past without a record made at the time.

concepts.title: Exemplum
concepts.summary: A story told to show conduct a reader should copy or avoid.

concepts.title: Traditional date
concepts.summary: A date given by later writers for an event that nobody recorded when it happened.

concepts.title: Consul
concepts.summary: One of two magistrates elected each year, in charge of public business at Rome and of the army in the field.

concepts.title: Senate
concepts.summary: The council of former magistrates, which controlled money, foreign relations and advice to the magistrates.

concepts.title: Assembly
concepts.summary: A meeting of citizens that elects magistrates, passes laws and decides on war and peace.

concepts.title: Veto
concepts.summary: A tribune's power to stop an act by saying 'I forbid'.

concepts.title: Mixed constitution
concepts.summary: A system in which monarchic, aristocratic and popular elements check one another, as Polybius describes Rome's.

concepts.title: The two orders
concepts.summary: Patricians, the old governing families, and plebeians, the other citizens, who for generations could not hold the main offices.

concepts.title: Secession
concepts.summary: A refusal by the plebeians to serve or to stay in the city until their demands were met.

concepts.title: The Twelve Tables
concepts.summary: Rome's first written laws, traditionally dated to about 450 BCE.

concepts.title: Change and continuity
concepts.summary: What a period altered and what it left as it was; both need evidence.

concepts.title: Ally
concepts.summary: A self-governing Italian community tied to Rome by treaty, which sent troops when the consuls asked.

concepts.title: Citizen levy
concepts.summary: An army raised each year from citizens who own property, rather than hired soldiers.

concepts.title: Colony
concepts.summary: A settlement of Roman citizens planted in conquered land, joined to Rome by roads.

concepts.title: Hedged report
concepts.summary: A claim a writer passes on while signalling that he does not vouch for it, with words such as 'there is a story' or 'it is said'.

concepts.title: Partisan source
concepts.summary: A source written by someone on one side of the matter it describes.

concepts.title: War guilt
concepts.summary: The question of which side is to blame for starting a war.

concepts.title: Hedged number
concepts.summary: A figure given with a sign that the writer cannot vouch for it, such as 'are said to have been'.

concepts.title: Authority
concepts.summary: The earlier writer a historian names as the source of a claim.

concepts.title: Corroboration
concepts.summary: Support for a claim from a second source that did not get it from the first.

concepts.title: Moral explanation
concepts.summary: An explanation of events by the habits and character of a people or its leaders.

concepts.title: Proletariat
concepts.summary: The landless working poor of the city of Rome, as the textbook uses the word.

concepts.title: Interpretation
concepts.summary: An account that selects facts and weighs them to explain what happened.

concepts.title: Later account
concepts.summary: An account written long after the events, built on earlier sources, some of which it names.

concepts.title: Chain of testimony
concepts.summary: The line from an event to the reader: who saw it, who told whom, who wrote it down.

concepts.title: Tribune
concepts.summary: An official elected by the plebeians who could propose laws and stop the acts of others.

concepts.title: Client army
concepts.summary: An army whose soldiers are more loyal to their commander, who promises them pay and land, than to the state.

concepts.title: Proscription
concepts.summary: A published list of men whom anyone might kill, and whose property was seized.

concepts.title: Dictator
concepts.summary: An old office that gave absolute authority for a limited time to meet an emergency.

concepts.title: Conspiracy
concepts.summary: A secret plan by a group to seize power or overthrow the government.

concepts.title: Triumvirate
concepts.summary: A private alliance of three men; the first, in 60 BCE, joined Pompey, Crassus and Caesar.

concepts.title: Claimed impartiality
concepts.summary: A writer's statement that he has no interest in the matter, which is itself something he chose to say.

concepts.title: Commentary
concepts.summary: Caesar's own report of his campaigns, written in the third person for readers at Rome.

concepts.title: Count and census
concepts.summary: A figure Caesar gives from a list or count; the question is who made it.

concepts.title: Justification
concepts.summary: A reason a writer gives for an action, chosen to persuade.

concepts.title: Res Gestae
concepts.summary: Augustus's own list of what he had done, set up on bronze columns in Rome.

concepts.title: Principate
concepts.summary: The system Augustus created, in which a first citizen held power through the old offices.

concepts.title: Facade
concepts.summary: An outward form kept after the substance has changed.

lessons.title: Founding stories and what Livy knew

lead.text: Roman tradition gives the city two dates on which every later account hangs. The first is 753 BCE, when the twin brothers Romulus and Remus are said to have founded it, and the second is 509 BCE, when the last king was driven out and the Romans declared their government a republic. Nobody recorded either event when it happened, so a date handed down in this way is called a **traditional date**, and the story behind it a **tradition**, which means something passed on about the past with no record made at the time.

The textbook says as much about the first date, because it writes that the city was founded in 753 BCE *according to Roman tradition*. Later in the same chapter it gives the second date as *around* 500 BCE, and we will see why when it turns from the story to what historians make of it.

afterFigure.text: The figure puts the two dates on a line of years counting down towards our own era, and its second view adds the man who wrote the story down. Livy began his history around 28 BCE, nearly five centuries after the second date and more than seven after the first.

diagram.alt: A line of years BCE from 800 to 0 with two traditional dates marked, 753 BCE for the founding of Rome and 509 BCE for the last king driven out. A second view adds Livy beginning to write about 28 BCE.
diagram.caption: The two dates are traditional. Use the buttons to see how long after them Livy wrote.

reveal.text: Livy gives the tales a place in his book and withholds his own guarantee. The next screen looks at the habits of wording by which he does that.

lead.text: Livy's story of the she-wolf shows the habit at work. He writes that *the tradition is* that a she-wolf found the exposed twins and nursed them, and that *it is said* the shepherd who took them in was called Faustulus. In the next breath he adds that *some are of opinion* the wolf was a woman the shepherds called Lupa, because she was a common prostitute, and that this is how the surprising story began. Each of those phrases hands the claim back to someone else, and the last one offers a plain explanation for the wonder.

A writer who does this is *reporting* a [[tradition|A story handed down about the past without a record made at the time. Met in 'Two traditional dates'.]] and not *vouching* for it. He has a reason to report it, which his preface gives: he wants readers to follow the Romans' conduct, from the men and measures that built the empire to the decline of its morals, and to choose from it what to copy and what to avoid. A story told to show conduct of that kind is called an **exemplum**, and much of what Livy tells about the early city is told as one.

reveal.text: A speech given to a woman in 509 BCE and written down nearly five centuries later shows what its writer chose to put in her mouth. The next screen says what that is good evidence of.

lead.text: Livy tells of Sextus Tarquin, the king's son, who wronged Lucretia, and of her death by her own hand once her husband and father had sworn to avenge her. As an account of what happened in 509 BCE it has the weakness that every late account has: nobody who saw the events wrote them down, and the man who wrote the story was working nearly five centuries afterwards. It cannot tell us what Sextus did.

What it can tell us is what Livy's readers were ready to admire and expect, a woman who puts her honour above her life and a family who answer a wrong with an oath. The scene is an exemplum, and it is good evidence of the **values Romans of Livy's day wanted to find in their beginnings**. A legend that fails as evidence of the event can therefore still be strong evidence of the telling, so the reader should neither take the story as a record nor throw it away as worthless.

reveal.text: Livy says what changed in a single sentence: the consulship became annual, and the consuls kept the kings' powers and signs. The textbook sets that change inside a wider story, and neither account rests on a record made in 509 BCE.

lead.text: Archaeology offers a different kind of evidence. The textbook reports that a wall was found around the Palatine Hill in 1988, where Romulus is said to have built his fortification, and that Greek pottery from the same period turned up at the same place, which suggests that trade took place. These finds are things left from the time itself, so they can be examined and dated in ways that a scene in Livy cannot. On that basis the textbook says the founding accounts have at least some historical basis.

It is careful about how far that goes. It does not say that Romulus built the wall, and of the expulsion of the kings it says only that the story is loosely based on events in which the city freed itself from Etruscan rule and became independent around 500 BCE, so the tidy 509 becomes a round number once the textbook speaks as a historian and not as a teller of the tale.

afterFigure.text: The two kinds of evidence answer different questions. The stories show how Romans pictured their beginnings, and the finds say something about the place and what went on there, while neither gives us the king, the day or the oath.

reveal.text: The kings ruled 244 years on the tradition's own dates, for seven kings. Whether that figure means anything is the next question.

steps.headline: Livy gives the last three kings 38, 40 and 25 years. How long does that leave for the first four kings out of the 244?

workedSteps.text: Livy's summary of the first book gives Tarquinius Priscus 38 years, Servius Tullius 40 and the last Tarquin 25, so add the three reigns.
The traditional dates allow 244 years for the whole line of seven kings, so the first four share what is left after the three reigns are taken away. Work out how many years that is.

Four kings sharing 141 years average a little over 35 years each. That is a claim to examine and not a fact to accept, so ask where the reign lengths came from. Livy's summary does not say, and he began writing nearly five centuries after the last king.

reveal.text: Tradition and find can both concern the same hill. Telling them apart is the habit to carry into the rest of the course.

lessons.orientation: Tell a founding tradition from evidence for the events it describes, and say what Livy's telling of the early stories is good evidence of.
lessons.reviewLabel: Founding stories and what Livy knew
lessons.nextAction: Read how Polybius, a Greek writing about Rome, assigns powers to consuls, Senate and people, and weigh him as an outside observer.

blocks.text: Ask almost anyone when Rome began and they can tell you: 753 BCE, with the last king driven out in 509 BCE. The textbook that gives the first date adds a phrase that credits it to what the Romans themselves said, and that phrase tells us the date came from a story, written down by people who lived long after it.

The main teller of that story is Livy, who began his history of Rome around 28 BCE. So what did Livy know about a city founded more than seven centuries before he started to write, and what is a historian doing when he tells a story that he says he will not vouch for?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a founding story is evidence of, how to read a historian who reports a tale without vouching for it, and why 753 and 509 BCE are traditional dates.
intro.whyItMatters: Most of what this course asks about Rome rests on writers who came long after the events, so reading them well starts here.

recap.keyIdea: A founding story is good evidence of how and why it was told, and a historian who reports it may not be vouching for it.

blocks.text: Livy kept the early tales in his book and said plainly that he would neither affirm nor refute them. That makes them traditions that he passes on, and the Lucretia scene is evidence of what a Roman of his day thought worth admiring, not of what happened in 509 BCE.
Archaeology adds a second kind of evidence, which is why the textbook speaks of a historical basis and gives only a round date. Both 753 and 509 BCE remain traditional dates.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson reads Polybius, a Greek who described the working Republic from outside and had a reason of his own for what he said.

lessons.title: The constitution seen from outside

lead.text: Polybius came from the Achaean League in Greece, and when Rome defeated Macedon in 168 BCE he was among the Achaeans taken to Italy, where he was held until 151 BCE. In the sixth book of his Histories he describes how the Romans were governed, and he says why he is doing it: he wants his readers to see how, and under what sort of political system, nearly the whole known world came under Roman power in somewhat less than fifty-three years.

That question gives him a thesis. If the constitution is the reason for Rome's rise, he has to show that it was unusually well built, and every power he describes will be fitted into that case. He also writes for Greeks, and he treats the Greek republics as ground his readers already know, which tells us whom he is explaining Rome to. None of this is a reason to dismiss him. It is a reason to ask, as we go, which parts of his account we could check.

reveal.text: The number is his own choice of span, made to stress how fast Rome rose, and it comes from the years he decided to cover.

lead.text: Polybius's central claim is that the Roman constitution had three elements, each with sovereign powers, so evenly balanced that no one, not even a native, could say for certain whether it was an aristocracy, a democracy or a despotism. The answer changes with where you look. Look only at the **consuls**, the two magistrates elected each year, and it seems a despotism: at home they direct the whole administration, every other magistrate except the tribunes answers to them, and on campaign their power is all but absolute.

Look only at the **Senate**, the council of former magistrates, and it seems an aristocracy. Look only at the **assembly** of the people, the meeting of citizens that elects magistrates and passes laws, and it seems a democracy. A system in which these elements share power and hold one another in check is called a **mixed constitution**, and that is the claim Polybius makes for Rome.

afterFigure.text: The figure takes each body in turn and gives the verdict of an observer who looked at that body alone. The three verdicts disagree, and Polybius's point is that all three observers are partly right.

diagram.alt: Three circles for the consuls, the Senate and the people, joined by dashed lines. In each of three views one circle is highlighted with Polybius's verdict if you looked at that body alone: despotism, aristocracy or democracy.
diagram.caption: Each body, seen alone, looks like a different kind of government. Use the buttons to move between them.

reveal.text: Polybius places the control of money with the Senate, and it matters because a consul on campaign has to be fed and paid. The next screen follows that thread.

lead.text: Polybius's reply to the idea that the consul is a despot starts with the treasury. The quaestors cannot issue public money without a decree of the Senate, so a consul who wants corn, clothes and pay for his legions has to have the Senate behind him. The Senate can also send another consul to replace him at the end of the year, and it decides whether his victory is honoured with a triumph. The people are a second check, because they ratify or refuse terms of peace and treaties, and a consul who lays down his office must give an account of his administration before them.

The Senate is checked too. It cannot carry out a death sentence for an offence against the republic unless the people ratify its decree. The tribunes, who are bound to carry out the people's decrees, hold the sharpest check. If a tribune interposes his **veto**, which is the power to stop an act by saying *I forbid*, the Senate cannot pass a decree and cannot even hold a meeting. Polybius concludes that the Senate has to take the common people seriously.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets this out from two sides. In the first view the consul reaches for supplies and treaties and finds the Senate and the people in the way. In the second the Senate, with all its power, still depends on the people and can be stopped by a single tribune.

diagram.alt: Three circles for the consul, the Senate and the people. In the first view arrows show a consul needing a Senate decree for supplies and the people's ratification of treaties. In the second the Senate needs the people to ratify death sentences and can be stopped by a tribune's veto.

reveal.text: Most powers belonged to one body and were limited by another, and that pattern is what Polybius means by a balance.

lead.text: Polybius speaks of the people as one body, and a modern textbook shows how much that simplifies. Rome had three main assemblies: the Plebeian Assembly, which only plebeians attended and which elected the ten tribunes; the Tribal Assembly, which both orders attended and which elected the quaestors; and the Centuriate Assembly, which alone could declare war. The Centuriate Assembly voted in blocs, and a bloc's weight depended on how many centuries of soldiers it could afford to equip, so wealthier citizens had more votes.

The textbook adds two points that Polybius's picture of three balanced bodies leaves out. All elected officials joined the Senate for life when their term ended, and many of them expected to be senators, which is part of why they rarely ignored its advice. And a patron-client system tied poorer citizens to wealthier ones, whose clients voted as their patrons directed. Neither point refutes Polybius. Each shows what a balanced picture can hide when it is drawn by someone who wants to praise the balance.

reveal.text: Polybius names the power correctly and says little about how the votes were shared, which is the kind of gap a second source can fill.

lead.text: An outsider has one clear advantage, which is that Polybius can compare Rome with the Greek constitutions he knows, and he does so from the start of the book. He also has three limits that a reader should keep in view. He has a thesis, which is that the constitution caused the success. He writes for Greeks, so he explains Rome through Greek categories such as aristocracy, democracy and despotism. And he describes the system at one moment, which the translator's note places at the time of Cannae in 216 BCE, and he says himself that later changes would not affect the truth of what he describes.

So we can use Polybius for what he is well placed to know, such as the main offices and how they checked one another, and test the claims where his purpose is at stake, such as how balanced the system really was. He is evidence of how a thoughtful Greek understood Rome, and that evidence is useful even where his judgement needs a second source.

reveal.text: Agreement between two sources is worth most when each had its own way of knowing the fact.

lessons.orientation: Say which body held which power in the middle Republic, and weigh Polybius's description by who he was and what he wanted to explain.
lessons.nextAction: Use Livy's narrative and the Twelve Tables together to say what changed and what stayed the same in the early Republic.

blocks.text: Polybius, a Greek from the Achaean League, was taken to Italy in 168 BCE and held there until 151 BCE. In the sixth book of his Histories he sets out to explain how the Romans were governed, and his answer is that no single name fits: the two chief magistrates look like kings, the council of former magistrates like an aristocracy and the people like a democracy.

His description gives us the offices and who held which power. It is also written by an outsider, for Greek readers, with a thesis to prove, so we have two jobs at once: to learn who held which power, and to decide how far to trust the man who is telling us.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which body held which power in Polybius's account, and to weigh him as an outside observer with a purpose of his own.
intro.whyItMatters: Much of what we know about how the Republic worked comes through writers who explain it for someone else, so weighing the explainer comes with the facts.

recap.keyIdea: Each body's power was limited by another's, and Polybius's account is best used by asking what an outsider with a thesis was well placed to know.

blocks.text: In Polybius's description the consuls command, the Senate controls the money, the people ratify treaties and pass laws, and a tribune's veto can stop the Senate. Each body leans on another, and that is what he means by a mixed constitution.

He is an outsider who wants to show that the constitution caused Rome's rise, so his picture of balance is the part to test, and the textbook's account of wealth-weighted votes shows where a second source adds something.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson sets a narrative beside a law code to ask what the early Republic changed and what it left as it was.

lessons.title: The Struggle of the Orders and the Twelve Tables

lead.text: In the early Republic Roman citizens belonged to one of two **orders**. The patricians were the old governing families, and for a long time only they could hold public office or take a seat in the Senate, while the plebeians were the other citizens. For generations the plebeians worked to win equality before the law, and the long quarrel is called the Struggle of the Orders. Their strongest weapon came from the way Rome fought: when enemies threatened the city, the plebeians gained leverage by refusing to serve in the army until their demands were met.

Livy tells of one such refusal, which he places early in the Republic. The plebeians withdraw from the city to a hill, and the withdrawal is called a **secession**. Livy opens that story with a debtor, an old soldier who shows the crowd that his debts have cost him his farm and then his freedom. We have the story from a writer working more than four centuries later, and we also have a clause of the law code on the same problem, so we can ask what each one is evidence of.

reveal.text: The scene and the clause are about the same trouble, and they do different jobs. The next screen names the difference.

lead.text: The first Roman law code is known as the **Twelve Tables**, traditionally dated to about 450 BCE and published in the Forum so that every citizen could read it. Our text is a modern translation of fragments, so the clause numbers follow that edition. A code is a different kind of evidence from a narrative. A narrative says what its author thought happened and how he wanted the reader to feel about it, while a law says what someone meant to allow or forbid.

Table III shows the difference with debt. A man who has confessed a debt, or lost a judgment, has thirty days to pay. After that the creditor may bring him before the magistrate and, if nobody speaks as his protector, take him home and fasten him with fetters weighing at least fifteen pounds. If the prisoner has no food of his own, the creditor owes him a daily ration of a pound of meal. We learn exactly what the law allowed and what it required of the creditor. We learn nothing about how many debtors were ever fettered, and Livy's veteran cannot tell us either, because his scene is a picture drawn centuries later.

afterFigure.text: The figure gives each source a card with the same three lines. Notice that the two cards are evidence of different things, and that each ends with something it cannot show.

diagram.alt: Two cards about debt. The first describes Livy's scene of a veteran in debt: written about four centuries or more after the events, it is evidence of how a later Roman pictured the harm. The second describes the clause of Table III: traditionally about 450 BCE, it is evidence of what the law allowed.

reveal.text: A clause can show that the orders were apart in law, and it needs other evidence to show how people lived.

lead.text: In Livy's telling the first secession ends with a settlement. The commons are allowed magistrates of their own, with inviolable persons and the power to bring help against the consuls, and no patrician may hold the office. These are the tribunes. Livy adds that his sources disagree about how many were first chosen, which is the kind of admission that makes him easier to trust on the rest. The textbook adds the power for which the tribunes became known: if they saw any official or body taking action that would harm plebeians, they could say *veto*, and stop it.

Livy's order of events puts the withdrawal and the first tribunes before the story of the ten tables, which he says were passed at an assembly voting by centuries. The textbook places the plebeians' first strike in 450 BCE, tied to their demand that the laws be written down. Those are two tellings of the early steps, so this lesson gives the withdrawal no year. Later steps are firmer. From 367 BCE one of the two consuls each year had to be a plebeian, and after 287 BCE the laws of the plebeian assembly applied to all Roman citizens.

reveal.text: Eighty years is a long time to wait between two rights, and it shows that the Struggle was slow.

lead.text: Historians ask of any period what it changed and what it left as it was, and both questions need evidence. The Struggle changed a good deal. The laws were written down for all, plebeians won officers who could stop an act, the highest office had to open to them, and in the end their assembly could make law for everyone. By the third century BCE, the textbook says, plebeians could make laws, hold elected office and take seats in the Senate.

Yet some things carried on. Rome still had elected magistrates, a Senate and assemblies, and the textbook says that the Struggle did not bring equality to everyone, because what it gave was access to power for well-off plebeians. Livy, writing centuries later, calls the ten tables the source of all public and private law in his own day. The last of those is a claim by a late writer and not a record, so we count it as a continuity that Livy asserts.

steps.headline: Work out what Table III lets a creditor do, and what the clause leaves unsaid.

workedSteps.text: The clause gives a debtor who has confessed a debt, or lost a judgment, thirty days to pay.
After thirty days the creditor may bring him before the magistrate and, unless someone speaks as his protector, fasten him with at least fifteen pounds of weight.
If the prisoner has no food of his own, the creditor owes him a daily ration of a pound of meal.
Everything above is what the rule permits and requires. It is a statement of what a lawmaker meant, so it cannot count cases, and that is the job for another kind of source.

reveal.text: The same care applies to a narrative that admits its own doubts.

lessons.orientation: Use a narrative and a law code together to say what changed and what stayed the same in the early Republic, and what each is evidence of.
lessons.reviewLabel: The Struggle of the Orders and the Twelve Tables
lessons.nextAction: Explain how Rome came to rule Italy as a mix of conditions and policies, and weigh an ancient and a modern source on it.

blocks.text: Two kinds of evidence survive for the early Republic's long quarrel between patricians and plebeians, and they speak differently. One is Livy's narrative, with scenes written down more than four centuries after the events. The other is Rome's first written law code, which comes down to us in fragments and were never written to tell a story.

A narrative tells us what a later writer thought happened and how he wanted it felt, while a law tells us what someone meant to allow or forbid. If we put the two beside each other on the same problem, debt, we can see what each is evidence of, and from there what changed in the early Republic and what carried on.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a narrative and a law each show about the same problem, and to sort the early Republic's changes from its continuities.
intro.whyItMatters: Laws, speeches and scenes all survive from Rome, and each answers a different question, so knowing which to ask of which is half of reading the period.

recap.keyIdea: A narrative and a law are evidence of different things, and a period is understood by asking what it changed and what it left as it was.

blocks.text: Livy's veteran shows how a later Roman pictured the harm of debt, and Table III shows what the law allowed a creditor to do. Neither is a count of cases.
The Struggle changed who could write, hold and make the law, from the written Tables to the binding assembly laws of 287 BCE, and it left Rome's governing bodies and much inequality in place.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from law to the system that made Rome master of Italy, and asks which of its causes were conditions and which were choices.

lessons.title: How Rome came to rule Italy

lead.text: Rome lay on a coastal plain called Latium, with the foothills of the Apennines to the east, where warlike tribes made periodic raids. The textbook says the early Romans had no plan to build a huge empire. Hostile city-states and tribes surrounded them, and each victory made new enemies while it widened their network of allies, so they kept sending armies farther afield against the next threat, until in the second century BCE Rome was the most powerful state on the Mediterranean.

That account has two kinds of explanation in it. Some of it describes what Rome faced, the neighbours and the raids, which were there before any Roman decision and made the outcome possible. These we call **conditions**, and we met the idea in the History course. The rest describes what Rome did, and each of those choices, repeated, shaped the result. We call these **policies**. A good account of Rome's rise keeps the two kinds apart, because the first tells us what made the outcome possible and the second tells us what Rome did with the chance.

reveal.text: Colonies and roads were something Rome built. The next screen lists the rest of the methods the textbook names.

lead.text: The textbook lists several methods, and a few of them were choices about whom to fight and when to make peace. Rome aimed to beat one enemy at a time, keeping its enemies from joining forces, often by setting them against each other, which is the old policy of divide and conquer. After even a severe defeat it continued the war until it had won a major engagement, so that it could negotiate with momentum on its side.

Other methods built something lasting. A **colony** was a settlement of Roman citizens planted in recently conquered land, a first line of defence if a region revolted, and roads linked the colonies to Rome so that armies could arrive quickly. Beaten peoples were turned into **allies**, self-governing communities tied to Rome by treaty. They kept their government so long as they honoured Rome's other alliances and sent troops in time of war, and some even received Roman citizenship.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows two rings around Rome. In the first view the inner ring is the colonies, and in the second the outer ring is the allied cities, with what Rome offered and what it asked.

diagram.alt: Rome drawn as a small circle at the centre of two rings. The inner ring marks colonies of Roman citizens joined to Rome by roads. The outer ring marks allied cities that kept self-government and sent troops. Each view explains one ring.

reveal.text: Two of the six describe the setting, and four describe what Rome did about it.

lead.text: Polybius takes us inside the machinery. Every year, he says, the consuls name a day for every citizen of military age to report, and the men are divided into four legions. Each legion is made up of 4,200 infantry, or 5,000 when the danger is special, and 300 horse. An army raised each year from the citizens themselves, and not from hired soldiers, is a **citizen levy**.

Letters go out as well to the officials of the allied Italian cities, telling them how many men are wanted and where and when to send them. The allies raise their own troops in much the same way, and each contingent has its own commander and paymaster. This is how an alliance worked in practice: Rome fixed the numbers and the day, and each ally did the enrolling.

afterFigure.text: The figure gives the two sizes of one legion. The totals are left for the next screen.

steps.headline: Work out how many men Polybius's four ordinary legions hold, counting the horse.

workedSteps.text: One legion holds 4,200 infantry and 300 horse, so add the two.
There are four legions in the levy, so multiply by four. Work out the total.
The allied cities' own troops are raised in addition, so this number is a floor and not the size of the whole army.

lead.text: Polybius uses the levy to explain something else. Carthage, he says, relied on foreign mercenaries and Rome on the valour of its own citizens and the aid of its allies, so even if the Romans lost at first they could start the war again at full strength, which the Carthaginians could not. The Romans, he adds, fight for country and children and persist until they have overcome their enemies.

We now have two accounts of the same system. The textbook is a modern summary that lists methods, and Polybius is an ancient writer who shows one of them, the levy and the allied contingents, in operation. Each needs weighing as we did in the last lesson. The textbook is only as good as the sources behind it, and it does not name them here. Polybius is a Greek with a thesis who describes the system at one moment, so his explanation of why Rome kept fighting is a claim to test, though his account of how the levy was organised is the kind of detail an observer is well placed to know.

reveal.text: Livy tells the story as a tradition about the 700s BCE. The tale fits what Rome later did, which is a reason to ask when it was told, and not a reason to believe it.

lead.text: The sources here are strong on how the system worked and on why historians think it succeeded. They are thin on the wars that built it. The passages in this course give no narrative of the Latin, Samnite or Pyrrhic wars and no dates for them, so we cannot say which colony was planted when, or which ally joined after which battle. The first war the textbook dates is the First Punic War, which began in 264 BCE, and it says that came after Rome had conquered most of the Italian peninsula.

That gap is part of the lesson. The textbook's claim that Rome did not plan an empire is an interpretation of a long chain of wars, and the chain itself is not in front of us. The more a conclusion depends on events we cannot see, the more cautiously it should be held. What we can say is how the machinery worked, which parts of it were Rome's choice, and which parts of the story were told centuries later to flatter the city's image of itself.

reveal.text: A choice and the means that made it workable can appear in different sources without any conflict.

lessons.orientation: Explain Roman expansion in Italy as a mix of conditions and policies with no master plan, and say what each source can and cannot show about it.
lessons.reviewLabel: How Rome came to rule Italy
lessons.nextAction: Separate the conditions, causes and trigger of the Second Punic War, and show where Livy's account takes Rome's side.

blocks.text: Italy held many cities with armies of their own, and one of them came to give orders to the rest. The usual first answers are that the Romans were better soldiers or that they had a plan, and neither fits the sources well. The textbook says the early Romans had no plan to build a huge empire: hostile city-states and tribes surrounded them, and every war they won made new enemies.

So how do we explain a result that nobody planned? We will split the explanation into what Rome faced and what Rome did, and then look at two very different sources on how the system worked, a modern summary and an ancient description with numbers in it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to separate the conditions Rome faced from the policies it chose, work from a source's own numbers, and say what a modern summary and an ancient description each offer.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every large change in the past has a setting nobody chose and a set of choices people made, and explanations improve when the two are kept apart.

recap.keyIdea: Rome's rise in Italy came from conditions it faced and policies it chose, and each source on it shows only part of that.

blocks.text: Hostile neighbours were conditions, and divide and conquer, fighting on after defeats, colonies with roads and self-governing allies were policies. Polybius's numbers show the citizen levy and the allied contingents at work, and the textbook gives the wider list of methods.
Neither source gives the wars themselves, and Livy's Romulus story shows how Romans of a later age pictured their city's growth.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes the same split to the Second Punic War and asks which grievances were conditions, which were causes and which set the war off.

lessons.title: Why the Second Punic War began

lead.text: Rome and Carthage fought two great wars within a lifetime of each other. The **First Punic War**, which ran from 264 to 241 BCE, was a fight for the island of Sicily, and it ended when Carthage, its fleet destroyed, asked for peace and Rome annexed the island. The **Second Punic War** began in 218 BCE, when the Carthaginian general Hannibal marched an army out of Hispania, across southern Gaul and over the Alps into Italy.

afterFigure.text: The textbook that gives these dates adds a line about motive, that after the first war Carthage wanted revenge. A line like that is a summary, written by someone who was not there and who gives no evidence for it, so it tells us what the question is and cannot answer it. The decisive battle of the second war, at Zama, is dated 202 BCE, and the war itself 218 to 201 BCE.

reveal.text: Livy's story begins in the gap between the two wars, and the next screen is about what he says went on in it.

lead.text: Livy opens his account of the Second Punic War by telling us how the two sides felt. The hatred between them, he says, was out of proportion to what each side could field: the Romans were indignant that people they had beaten should take up arms against their conquerors, while the Carthaginians believed that in defeat they had been ruled with haughtiness and avarice. He gives each side a grievance, and he puts the Carthaginian one in terms the Carthaginians themselves might have used.

He then names one man. Hamilcar, Hannibal's father, was grieved at the loss of Sicily and Sardinia, because he thought Sicily had been given up too early, in a premature despair, and that the Romans had treacherously taken Sardinia while Africa was in disorder. On top of that Carthage had been made to pay a tribute.

afterFigure.text: Livy does not say that all this was true. He says what Hamilcar thought, and the thought is a Carthaginian's, passed to us by a Roman who was writing about two centuries after the war began.

reveal.text: Livy's next claim is of a different kind from the grievances above, and the next screen says why.

lead.text: Livy's phrase 'there is besides a story' is a signal worth learning to read. A writer who says 'it is said' or 'there is a story' is passing on a claim while telling you that he does not vouch for it, and we call such a claim a **hedged report**. Livy does not say who told the story of the oath, and nobody could have watched a boy of about nine make a vow at an altar and then written it down in a form that survived to Livy's day, so he has no way to check it.

The hedge tells us what we can do with the story. We can use it as evidence that Romans told a tale in which Hannibal hated Rome from childhood, which says something about how they explained the war, and we can decline to use it as an explanation of why the war began, because nothing in the passage shows that anyone swore anything. The same passage carries no hedge on Hamilcar's grief: Livy states Hamilcar's grief about Sicily and Sardinia in plain words. An unhedged claim may still be wrong; the writer is at least putting his name to it.

afterFigure.text: Livy was writing about two centuries after the war began. The dating of his whole work is given as about 26 BCE to 15 CE, and the war began in 218 BCE, so even the grievances reach him at long distance.

lead.text: You met three kinds of factor in the History course, and the Punic wars give us a case to use them on. A **condition** is part of the background that stays in place for years and makes an event possible without making it happen. A **cause** pushes the event along, and is often a decision to act. A **trigger** is the single event that sets it off once everything else is ready.
The three are not rivals. A war can have all of them, and a historian's task is to say which factor is which and to give the reason.

afterFigure.text: Because the three differ in how long they last and when they happen, two questions place almost any factor: how long had it been true before the event, and did it happen on one particular day? A long-standing feeling answers the first, a decision answers neither, and the last step answers the second.

steps.headline: Place Hamilcar's grief over Sicily and Sardinia as a condition, a cause or a trigger.

workedSteps.text: First ask how long the grievance had been in place. Sicily was given up in 241 BCE, and the war began in 218 BCE.
Then ask whether the grief was one event on one day. Livy describes it as a standing resentment, not a happening.
Name the kind of factor that has lasted for years and is not an event.

lead.text: Livy's account of what pushed the war along starts from a decision. From the day he was declared general, he says, Hannibal resolved to make war on the people of Saguntum. He knew, Livy adds, that an attack on Saguntum would bring the Romans to arms, so he first led his army against another people, the Olcades, so that he might seem to have been drawn on by events.

That is a claim about intention, and intentions are the hardest things to know. We can see where an army marched, and Livy's own account of it is probably a fair guide to the movements. What Hannibal meant by marching there, and what he wanted others to think, was in his own head, and Livy reports it as if he had been told.

afterFigure.text: Livy also stops, in the same book, to argue over which year Saguntum fell and which consuls were in office, and he works through the possibilities without settling them. A writer who is unsure of the order of events has a harder time knowing what was in one man's mind.

reveal.text: The decision to attack Saguntum is still, in Livy's account, a cause. The question is how firmly he can claim to know it.

lead.text: Livy says that Rome sent envoys to Carthage to ask whether Hannibal had besieged Saguntum by public authority, and to declare war if Carthage owned it. In the reply Livy gives to a Carthaginian, the real question is whether the attack broke a treaty. The treaty made with Hasdrubal excepted the Saguntines, the speaker says, and Rome had once denied being bound by a treaty because the senate and people had not authorised it, so a treaty made by Hasdrubal without Carthage's knowledge could not bind Carthage either. The Roman envoy then folded his robe, said he carried both peace and war, and when the Carthaginians told him to give whichever he chose, he gave war.

Then Livy gives his own view, and this is where a partisan source shows itself. He says that Rome's plain approach of making inquiry and then denouncing war suited its dignity better than quibbling over what the treaties required. A neutral reporter would say what each side argued. Livy says which way of arguing was worthier, and it is Rome's.

afterFigure.text: A **partisan source** is written by someone on one side of what it describes, and the right response is neither to throw it out nor to accept it. Livy shows us the Carthaginian argument and does not hide the Carthaginian grievances, which is useful. We then watch for the places where his language leans, and we discount those places.

reveal.text: Placing the factors this way is Livy's picture, and Carthage's version would likely have put the weight elsewhere.
Livy gave the Carthaginian side a voice, and he still chose the words, so what we hear is an argument of the kind Carthage made as heard by Rome.

lessons.orientation: Sort what led to the Second Punic War into conditions, causes and a trigger, and find where Livy takes Rome's side.
lessons.reviewLabel: Why the Second Punic War began
lessons.nextAction: Read a casualty figure in Livy and Polybius for who counted it and how sure the writer is.

blocks.text: Livy begins his account of the second war between Rome and Carthage with a claim about feelings. The hatred with which the two sides fought, he says, was almost greater than their resources, and he goes on to say what each side felt and why. A war that comes out of feelings raises a question that every war raises, which is who began it.

The question is harder to answer when the historian belongs to one of the two sides, as Livy, a Roman, does. We have to separate what led to the war over many years from what set it off, and we have to notice where the writer's own loyalty enters the sentence. Livy gives us enough to do both.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to sort the things that led to the war into conditions, causes and a trigger, and to point to places where Livy takes Rome's side.
intro.whyItMatters: Most of what survives about this war was written by Romans, so reading a side's account carefully is a skill you will use in every lesson that follows.

recap.keyIdea: A war has conditions, causes and a trigger, and a partisan source such as Livy needs reading for the places where he leans towards his own side.

blocks.text: Livy gives Carthage real grievances, loss of Sicily and Sardinia and a tribute among them, and he marks the oath as a story he passes on without vouching for it. He treats Hannibal's plan as a cause but claims knowledge of an intention that nobody could have reported to him.
When he finishes by saying that the Roman way of declaring war was the more fitting, he stops being a reporter and takes a side, and that is the place a careful reader slows down.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows Hannibal into Italy and asks how much weight to give a number in an ancient historian, using Livy's figures for the dead at Cannae.

lessons.title: Hannibal in Italy and the numbers at Cannae

lead.text: In the English translation of Livy used in this course, forty thousand Roman foot soldiers and two thousand seven hundred horse are said to have been killed at Cannae, with as many citizens as allies among them. Other editions of the Latin may give a different figure, so treat it as one reading and not a settled count. Polybius, in his own account, says that of the infantry about ten thousand were taken prisoner, that about three thousand escaped, and that all the rest died, to the number of seventy thousand. The gap between 40,000 (in this translation of Livy) and 70,000 is the difference between two writers, and neither was alive in 216 BCE, since Polybius was born around 200 BCE and Livy in 59 BCE.

So each figure is a claim by its author, and we will treat it as one. Neither is a count made on the field, and nothing in the two accounts lets us choose between them. What we can do is ask what each writer's wording tells us about how sure he was.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the two foot-soldier counts to the same scale. Livy's figure in this translation is about four sevenths of Polybius's, and the question for a historian is which words around the numbers show how each writer came by them.

diagram.alt: Horizontal bars for the number of Roman foot soldiers killed at Cannae. Livy's bar, the figure in this translation, is 40,000 and Polybius's is 70,000, about 1.75 times longer.
diagram.caption: Two writers, two numbers for one battle. Use the buttons to look at each, then both together.

reveal.text: Livy's figure is a total of two groups, and the next screen asks what the wording around that total says.

lead.text: A number in an ancient history comes with a sign of how much the writer stands behind it. Livy's account of the lake Trasimenus shows the range. He gives fifteen thousand Romans slain and fifteen hundred of the enemy, which is ten to one, and then says that some authors report the carnage as many times greater. He does not average them. He says he will not use a worthless source, to which historians' minds incline too much, and that his chief authority is Fabius, who lived through the war.

The earlier writer a historian names as the source of a claim is called an **authority**. Naming one lets a reader follow the number back and see how close it stands to the event. When a writer gives a number without naming anyone and writes that it 'is said' or 'they reckon', the figure is a **hedged number**, because the words around it say that he cannot vouch for it.

afterFigure.text: Cannae is the harder case, because Livy's sentence about the dead comes with a hedge and names no authority. The figure on this screen puts his two battles side by side.

reveal.text: Livy carries the same sign of caution through the rest of the passage, and the next screen shows a place where he carries it a step further.
Livy followed the remark by saying that the delay is firmly believed to have saved the city, and the next screen explains why that wording matters.

lead.text: Behind every claim there is a line of people, from whoever saw it to the writer who set it down, and a claim is only as good as the weakest link in that line. For Maharbal's remark the first link is the tent where Hannibal and his officer talked. Nobody on the Roman side was in it, and Livy was writing about 190 years after Cannae, from 216 BCE to the start of his work around 26 BCE, so the remark reached him from some chain of retelling that he does not describe.

Look also at what Livy claims for it. The delay, he says, is firmly believed to have saved the city, which is a statement about what people think and not a record of what happened. The remark is a good story and it explains a puzzle, why Hannibal did not march on Rome, which is just the kind of thing that gets said afterwards and attached to a famous man.

afterFigure.text: A second source would help, provided it did not get the story from Livy. This is **corroboration**: support from a second source that did not take the claim from the first. For Maharbal's remark we have none in these texts, and so we hold it as a story.

lead.text: Polybius makes a larger claim about the aftermath. He says that when the Senate refused to ransom the prisoners, Rome was, roughly speaking, deprived of all its allies, and still neither yielded to misfortune nor neglected what became it. He gives the Senate's reasoning: Hannibal wanted money and wanted to take away the enthusiasm of the Roman troops by showing that even the conquered could get home, so the Senate showed no pity even to the prisoners' own families, and made it a rule that Romans must win or die on the field.

The textbook says almost the opposite. It says that Hannibal hoped Rome's allies would desert it, and that most of the Italian allies stayed loyal even after Cannae. The two sentences cannot both describe the same thing in the same sense.

afterFigure.text: They could still both be true. Polybius's 'roughly speaking' tells us he is rounding, and 'allies' may mean different peoples in the two accounts, or the same peoples at different months. Polybius wrote in the second century BCE, much closer to the war than the textbook, but being closer does not by itself settle what he meant.

reveal.text: Which account is closer in time is only one thing to weigh, and the next lessons take up the others.
Livy's book order carries the sequence, and the textbook supplies the date of the last battle.

lessons.orientation: Read a casualty figure for who counted it and how sure the writer is, and compare two accounts of Rome's allies.
lessons.reviewLabel: Hannibal in Italy and the numbers at Cannae
lessons.nextAction: Compare three explanations of the Republic's troubles and say which parts are fact, evidence or interpretation.

blocks.text: At Cannae in 216 BCE a Carthaginian army under Hannibal destroyed the largest Roman army of the war, and the translation of Livy used here puts a number on the cost: forty thousand foot soldiers and two thousand seven hundred horse, a figure that other editions of the Latin may read differently. Polybius, who wrote earlier, says that seventy thousand foot soldiers died. Neither man was alive at the time, since Polybius was born around 200 BCE and Livy in 59 BCE.

Numbers in ancient histories look precise and are often guesses, and some are repeated from one book to the next until they harden into fact. What does a figure tell us about the battle, and what does it tell us only about the writer?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a number in an ancient history for who gave it and how sure he sounds, and to set two accounts of one fact side by side.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every ancient battle comes to us as a number and a story. Asking where each came from is the first step in judging either.

recap.keyIdea: A number in an ancient history is a claim by its writer, and the words around it, and the authority named for it, show how far to trust it.

blocks.text: Livy's 42,700 at Cannae, the figure in this translation, comes with 'are said to have been', which marks it as a figure he passes on, while at Trasimene he names Fabius, a contemporary, as the writer he follows. Maharbal's remark has no authority and no second source, so it is a story, and Polybius and the textbook disagree about Rome's allies in a way that first needs the meanings of their words checked.
The battles themselves fall in order: the Trebia, Trasimene, Cannae, then Zama after a gap of fourteen years.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from the war to what it did to Rome, and asks how to tell a fact from an interpretation in three writers' explanations.

lessons.title: What empire did to Rome

lead.text: Polybius describes Rome at its height, and one of his points of comparison is money. In Carthage, he says, nothing is disgraceful that makes for gain, and the Carthaginians obtain office by open bribery. At Rome, he says, nothing is more disgraceful than taking bribes or profiting by improper means, and the penalty for bribery for office is death. The translator's note places the state he describes around the time of Cannae, 216 BCE.

That is a claim about law and custom, made by a Greek who admires the system and wants his readers to understand why Rome won, and Carthage is his foil. He could be right about the law and still be describing an ideal more than a practice.

afterFigure.text: A rule that bribery is punished by death is evidence that the Romans had a rule. It is weaker evidence about how often anyone was caught.

lead.text: Sallust tells a story that seems to point the other way. Jugurtha, a king of Numidia in North Africa, was ordered by the senate to leave Italy, and as he went, he is said, after looking back at the city in silence, to have exclaimed that it was a venal city that would soon perish if it could find a purchaser. The war with Jugurtha, according to the textbook, began in 112 BCE, and Sallust wrote about it in 41 to 40 BCE.

So the two writers stand at different places. Polybius is describing Rome at its height, and Sallust is describing a war that came after the destruction of Carthage and Corinth in 146 BCE and was written down in the 40s BCE. The phrase 'is said' matters here: Sallust passes the remark on as a story, as Livy passed on the oath.

afterFigure.text: The figure puts the three moments on one line, because most of the confusion comes from forgetting that the two writers are not describing the same year.

steps.headline: Work out how many years there are from the destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE to the war with Jugurtha in 112 BCE.

workedSteps.text: Years BCE count down towards the present, so 112 BCE is the later date and has the smaller number.
The gap is the difference between the two numbers.
Work out the difference and say how many years separate the two events.

reveal.text: The next screen takes up the explanation Sallust himself gives for a change in the Roman state.

lead.text: Sallust gives an explanation, and he gives it twice, in two different books. Before the destruction of Carthage, he says, the senate and people ran the state with mutual moderation, and the dread of an enemy kept it in order. When that fear was removed, licentiousness and pride, which prosperity loves to foster, began to prevail, and peace proved more grievous than adversity. In his other book he adds that once Carthage was destroyed and the seas lay open, ease and wealth became a burden, and the love of money and then of power became the source of every evil.

This is a **moral explanation**: it explains events by the habits and character of a people. It is also an **interpretation**, an account that selects facts and weighs them to say what happened. Both are legitimate, and neither is a fact. Sallust offers no test of his explanation in these passages. He does not show that quarrels were fewer before 146 BCE, and he does not say what he would count as evidence against it.

afterFigure.text: The claim is plausible, which is why it is worth testing. A claim that something changed after a certain year can be checked by comparing sources from before and after.

reveal.text: Sallust's explanation and the textbook's are different in kind, as the next screen shows.

lead.text: The textbook explains the troubles differently. From the foundation of the republic, it says, most Roman citizens had owned and worked small family farms, and men had to own property to serve as soldiers. The Punic Wars strained that system: soldiers were away for long periods, their families struggled to keep the holdings, and many on returning found their property in another's hands, or sold their farms and moved to Rome. There they joined the landless working class that the textbook calls the **proletariat**.

The textbook adds a number: after the defeat of Perseus in 168 BCE, 150,000 people from Epirus were enslaved by the Romans, and on Delos ten thousand people were reportedly sold on a single day. Neither number comes with a count in the passage. They are figures passed on, and the textbook marks the second as such.

afterFigure.text: Compare this explanation with Sallust's. The textbook points to what soldiers lost, farms and families. Sallust points to what citizens gained, wealth and safety, and what it did to their character.

reveal.text: The textbook gives its figure with a hedge in the same way that Livy did, and the same question applies.

lead.text: Polybius, too, has a moral explanation, and he gave it as a forecast. In his view, the desire of office, the shame of losing reputation, and ostentation and extravagance of living would begin a deterioration. People who felt cheated by some and flattered by others would refuse to be content with equal powers, demand to have all or most of them, and call the result liberty or democracy when it was in fact mob-rule.

That tells us that moral explanations of Roman decline were not invented afterwards by Sallust. They were already a way of thinking in Polybius's day, and a historian reading Sallust has to ask how much of his account comes from the evidence and how much from a pattern he already held.

afterFigure.text: The figure lays the three explanations side by side: what each says went wrong, what evidence the passage offers for it, and where each writer stood.

lessons.orientation: Compare three explanations of Rome's troubles and say which parts are fact, evidence or interpretation.
lessons.nextAction: Weigh a biographer writing long after the events by tracing where each of his claims comes from.

blocks.text: Polybius, writing of Rome at its height, says that at Rome the penalty for buying office is death. Sallust, writing in the 40s BCE, tells a story in which a king leaves the city saying it could be bought if only a purchaser appeared. The two statements are about the same city and seem to disagree.

They are also two of the three explanations that this lesson reads for what went wrong with Rome after its wars, and the third, a modern textbook's, points somewhere else again. What can we do with three accounts of one change, written at three distances from it?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say, for three explanations of Rome's troubles, which parts are fact, evidence or interpretation, and what each writer could see from where he stood.
intro.whyItMatters: Every large change in history has several explanations. Knowing what kind of claim each one is makes them possible to compare.

recap.keyIdea: An explanation of a historical change is an interpretation, and it should be read for what the writer could see, what evidence he offers and what he sets aside.

blocks.text: Polybius, Sallust and the textbook each say what went wrong with Rome, and each is an interpretation: Polybius forecasts it from wealth and ambition, Sallust blames the end of fear of Carthage, and the textbook points to wars, farms and the landless poor. None of the three offers a test of its own explanation in the passages we read.
A statement of fact, such as the year Carthage fell, differs from what a source says and from an explanation built on it, and a figure marked 'reportedly' is one more claim to weigh.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows one reform in particular, Tiberius Gracchus's land law, through a biographer who wrote more than two centuries after it.

lessons.title: The Gracchi and a later biographer

lead.text: Plutarch, who wrote more than two centuries after the events, begins from a problem with land. Earlier limits on how much public land one man might hold had been evaded: rich men got the land back under other people's names, and in the end claimed most of it openly. The poor, deprived of their farms, were no longer ready to serve in war or careful about their children's education, until few free men were left in Italy, whose estates were crowded with foreign-born slaves.

Tiberius Gracchus proposed to change that. He was elected a **tribune**, an official elected by the plebeians who could propose laws and stop the acts of others, and in 133 BCE, according to the textbook, he put forward a law that would give public land to Romans who had none. The textbook's outline agrees with Plutarch's in shape: wars away from home, farms lost, large estates worked by enslaved people.

afterFigure.text: This agreement is some comfort, but it does not make Plutarch an eyewitness. He is a **later account**: written long after the events, from earlier sources, some of which he names. The next screens ask what he names, and what he does not.

lead.text: Plutarch does not give one reason for the law. He gives several, and he introduces each differently. The most common account, he says, is that two advisers pushed Tiberius to it, Diophanes the rhetorician and Blossius the philosopher. Some have also charged Cornelia, Tiberius's mother, who often reproached her sons that Romans still called her Scipio's daughter and not the mother of the Gracchi. Others say that Spurius Postumius, a rival speaker, gave the occasion, because Tiberius wanted to outdo him.

Then comes a different kind of claim. His brother Gaius, Plutarch says, left it in writing that Tiberius first formed the policy when he saw the countryside of Tuscany nearly empty of free farmers on his way to Numantia. And Plutarch adds, in his own voice, that it is most certain the people urged Tiberius on by setting up writings on porches, walls and monuments.

afterFigure.text: Look at the wording in the figure. Only one of the five names a document, and it is the brother's. The other four rest on 'most commonly stated', 'some', 'others' and Plutarch's own certainty.

reveal.text: The brother's writing is the one source that Plutarch names, and the next screen asks how such a source passes down.

lead.text: Any claim about the past reaches us along a line: someone saw or did something, someone told it or wrote it, someone else read that and wrote again, and at the end a reader opens a book. We call the whole line a **chain of testimony**, and a claim is only as good as its weakest link. Here the links run from Tiberius in 133 BCE, to his brother Gaius, who wrote about him, to Plutarch, writing about 105 to 115 CE, to a translator, and so to us.

The chain has a limit that no skill in reading can remove. Plutarch tells us Gaius wrote it; we cannot read Gaius's text ourselves, and the passage does not say when he wrote or whether he was present. What the chain lets us do is rank the claims by how near each could stand to Tiberius, and Gaius's writing is the nearest we have.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the links and what each could know. Gaius died in 121 BCE, so whatever he wrote about his brother was written before that year.

reveal.text: The brothers' careers fit inside twelve years, and Plutarch wrote more than two centuries after them.

lead.text: Plutarch also gives Tiberius a speech. 'The savage beasts in Italy,' he has Tiberius say, 'have their particular dens', but the men who bear arms and risk their lives for their country enjoy nothing more in it than the air and light, and wander with their wives and children for lack of houses. It is the best-known passage of the life, and it sounds as though someone had been taking notes.

The passage does not say where the words came from. Plutarch was writing more than two centuries later, and it names no record, no witness and no earlier writer for this speech, as it did for Gaius's account. A historian can still use it, because it shows how the argument was remembered and how Plutarch, or someone before him, wanted it to sound. It cannot be used to say what Tiberius said.

reveal.text: The same caution applies to anything in Plutarch that has no named source.

lead.text: Plutarch gives Tiberius a reason for the final step. When his fellow tribune Octavius would not give way, Tiberius declared that two men of equal authority in the same office could hardly settle so weighty a matter without civil war, and that the only remedy was to depose one of them. This, Plutarch writes, we are told, was the first quarrel among the Romans since the kings that ended in bloodshed, and all earlier quarrels had been settled by concessions on both sides.

Sallust, who wrote about a century after the Gracchi, tells it differently in his own war book. The nobility, alarmed and aware of their own guilt, tried to stop the Gracchi, and they killed Tiberius first and Gaius a few years later. Yet he adds that, in the Gracchi, from their ardour for victory, there was not sufficient prudence. Sallust blames violence by the nobility and also finds fault in the Gracchi.

afterFigure.text: Two accounts are a gain only if they are independent. Nothing in these passages says whether either writer used the other, so their agreement is worth less than it would be if we knew they did not.

reveal.text: Where two writers agree, the claim is better supported, and where they differ, the difference is the interesting part.
The same questions apply to any later account: who is named, who is not, what could be checked and what the writer wants.

lessons.orientation: Weigh a later account by following each claim back to its source and comparing a second writer.
lessons.reviewLabel: The Gracchi and a later biographer
lessons.nextAction: Explain how soldiers' loyalty moved from the state to their commanders under Marius and Sulla.

blocks.text: Plutarch tells us why Tiberius Gracchus proposed his land law in 133 BCE, and he gives more than one reason. Some say it was his mother, others say a rival, and Tiberius's own brother left it in writing that he was moved by an empty countryside. Plutarch was writing more than two centuries after the law, and he was not there.

A biography written so long afterwards is a source written long after the events. It can still be good evidence, because its author read earlier writers whose work has not survived. We have to follow each claim back to see who it came from and how near they were to the man. Who stands behind each of the reasons Plutarch gives?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a claim in a later account back to the source Plutarch names for it, and to say what a second writer adds.
intro.whyItMatters: Most of what we know about the distant past comes through later writers, so asking who told whom is the most useful question to bring to any of them.

recap.keyIdea: A later account is as good as its chain of testimony, so trace each claim back to the source the writer names and ask what could be checked.

blocks.text: Plutarch names one document for Tiberius's motive, his brother Gaius's writing, and gives the others as 'most commonly stated', 'some say' and 'others say'. His speech for Tiberius has no named source, so it shows how the argument was remembered more than what was said.

Sallust, writing nearer the events but from his own place, agrees that Tiberius died in violence and adds a fault to both sides, which is the kind of second account that makes the first easier to weigh.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows a general's soldiers and asks why they came to follow a commander and not the state.

lessons.title: Marius, Sulla and soldiers who followed a general

lead.text: Marius won the consulship for 107 BCE and, once elected, turned to raising an army. Sallust, who tells this in his *Jugurthine War*, was born in 86 BCE, the year Marius died, and wrote the book around 41 BCE. He wrote about a man he could never have known, and what he says came from earlier histories and memoirs, among them Sulla's, and from what he gathered in Numidia, which he had governed under Caesar.

Plutarch, who tells us about Sulla, was a Greek born about the middle of the first century CE, well over a century after the events he describes. The textbook is a modern summary. None of the three saw what happened, and each is doing a different job.

afterFigure.text: Sallust and Plutarch tell a story and report what people said about it. The textbook draws a conclusion from many such stories. It pays to keep those two jobs apart, because a conclusion can sound firmer than the stories under it.

diagram.alt: A timeline from 110 to 40 BCE. The first view marks Marius elected consul in 107 BCE, Sulla's march on Rome in 88 BCE, Marius's death in 86 BCE, Sulla becoming dictator in 82 or 81 BCE and resigning in 79 BCE. The second view marks Sallust's birth in 86 BCE, the year Marius died, and his writing about 41 BCE, with Plutarch far off the edge.
diagram.caption: Events on the first view, writers on the second. Sallust was born the year Marius died and wrote about 45 years later.

lead.text: Sallust has said that Marius took the poor. The next sentence is about why.

reveal.text: Sallust's remark about a man grasping at power says what the needy are useful for. Setting it among the things said keeps this a [[hedged report|A claim a writer passes on while signalling that he does not vouch for it, such as “it is said”. Met in “Why the Second Punic War began”.]], and the textbook's version has no such hedge.

lead.text: Sallust also gives Marius a speech, addressed to “my fellow-citizens”, in which Marius attacks the nobility. The nobles, he says, rely on the merits of their forefathers and demand every public honour as a right of birth, not of their own worth. Their ancestors left them riches, statues and glorious names, but could not leave them virtue, which Marius calls the one possession that cannot be passed on.

Is that what Marius said? J. C. Rolfe, in his introduction to the Loeb Classical Library edition of Sallust (1921), writes that the speeches in Sallust's books “do not purport to give the exact words of the speakers”. They are “carefully composed” to suit the speakers, he adds, “but the language is that of Sallust himself.” So the speech shows how Sallust pictured Marius's case, a self-made man set against inherited rank, and Rolfe also says that Sallust's leaning towards the popular party is “obvious”.

afterFigure.text: A speech in an ancient history is therefore **evidence of the historian's picture of the speaker**. It is good evidence for what Sallust, and the readers he wrote for, thought Marius stood for, and weak evidence for the words spoken on the day.

lead.text: Read the passage with Rolfe's remark in mind.

reveal.text: Rolfe says that Sallust's own leaning was towards the popular party, so a speech that sets Marius's merit against the nobles' names is what a reader should expect from him. That makes it better evidence of Sallust than of Marius.

lead.text: Now set Sallust beside the textbook. In its account Marius, once in power, reformed the army's entrance requirements so that [[proletariats|The landless working poor of the city of Rome, as the textbook uses the word. Met in “What empire did to Rome”.]] could join, which offered them a share of the spoils and even land in return for service. These reforms, it says, produced armies of professional soldiers who depended on their commanders.

The textbook's name for the result is a **client army**: an army whose soldiers are more loyal to their commander, who promises them war gains and land, than to the state. The textbook's proletariats and Sallust's men from the lowest ranks are probably the same men, but only the textbook gives them that name.

afterFigure.text: The table sets the ancient writers beside the textbook for three stages. Read the middle row with care. Plutarch says that Sulla's six legions were all willing to march on Rome while Sulla himself was still doubtful and afraid of the danger, whereas the textbook says Sulla convinced his soldiers. Both could be true, but they put the willingness in different places, and that matters for the question of whom the soldiers were following.
