The office had not been</text><text class="t-small" x="391.0" y="326" text-anchor="start">used since the Second Punic</text><text class="t-small" x="391.0" y="344" text-anchor="start">War.</text><text class="t-small t-muted" x="24" y="384" text-anchor="start">Shaded: the textbook says more, or more firmly, than the writer.</text></svg>

lead.text: Plutarch tells what Sulla did with his power. He posted lists of names, and the word for a list of that kind is a **proscription**: a published list of men whom anyone might kill, and whose property was seized. Plutarch's first list held eighty names. A day later Sulla added two hundred and twenty names, and on the day after that he added as many again.

Sulla then told the people that he had listed every name he could recall, and that any he had forgotten he would add later, so the lists had no fixed end. Sheltering a listed man became a capital offence, with no exception for a brother, son or parent, and killing one earned a reward of two talents, even when the killer was a slave who murdered his master or a son who murdered his father.

steps.headline: Work out how many names Plutarch says were on Sulla's first three lists.

workedSteps.text: Plutarch's first list holds eighty names.
After one day's respite he posts two hundred and twenty more, which makes two lists so far.
Then, “on the third again, as many”. Before adding anything, say what “as many” refers to.
Because the total rests on a reading of two English words, a historian records it as a reading of Plutarch and not as a number he states.

lead.text: Now finish the count.

reveal.text: Plutarch's own words are “eighty”, “two hundred and twenty” and “as many”. The total of 520 is a historian's sum over a reading of the third.

lead.text: Plutarch says that Sulla made himself dictator, an office that had been left unused for a hundred and twenty years. A **dictator** was, in the old republican sense, an officer given absolute authority for a limited time to deal with an emergency. The textbook says the office had not been used since the Second Punic War, which ended in 201 BCE, and Sulla took it in late 82 or early 81 BCE. Count back 120 years from 81 BCE and you reach 201, so the two writers agree. The textbook does not say where its date comes from, so it may be repeating the same tradition, but the figure survives the test it can be given.

Plutarch also reports an act that forgave what Sulla had already done and, for the future, gave him power over life and death, over confiscation and the division of land, over founding and razing cities, and over taking away kingdoms and giving them to whom he pleased. Those are not the powers of a man sent to deal with one emergency, though we should remember that Plutarch is our witness to the list. The textbook adds that Sulla gave up the office in 79 BCE.

afterFigure.text: The office keeps its old name, which is continuity, while the gap of 120 years, the special act and the years for which one man held it mark a change. A historian can say both.

lead.text: Apply that to the passage itself.

reveal.text: The name of the office was the thread, and everything around it was new. That is why a historian says the dictatorship changed even though the word stayed.

lead.text: Three things could be the new thing in the break between army and state. One is the soldiers themselves, men from the lowest ranks, whom Sallust says Marius took in 107 BCE. Another is the commander's promises, since the textbook says Marius offered war gains and land and that Sulla, like him, promised his recruits land. The third is the willingness to use the army inside Italy, which Plutarch shows in 88 BCE, when six legions were ready to march against the city, and which the textbook says happened again in 87 BCE when Marius marched on Rome.

The sources do not weigh these for us, and the textbook's sentence about client armies folds them into one. What we can do is ask how firmly each rests. That an army marched on Rome is reported by Plutarch and agreed by the textbook. That poor men were enlisted is reported by Sallust, who is unsure why. That the promise of land made the soldiers loyal to their general is the textbook's conclusion, and neither passage we read says it outright.

afterFigure.text: So the events are firmer than the causes. A historian can say with some confidence that soldiers followed their generals into Rome, and with much less that the promise of land is why.

lead.text: Here is the same distinction, between a report and a conclusion, in a case made up for the purpose.

reveal.text: In each case the conclusion could be right. It has a different standing from the report, because it was drawn by someone who knew how things turned out.

lessons.orientation: Separate what Sallust and Plutarch report about Marius and Sulla from what the textbook concludes, and judge how firmly each claim rests.
lessons.reviewLabel: Marius, Sulla and soldiers who followed a general
lessons.nextAction: Read Sallust's account of Catiline for its author's purpose, and check it against Plutarch.

blocks.text: Sallust says that when Marius raised his army for the war against King Jugurtha he set the old method aside and took any man willing to join him, most of them from the lowest ranks. A modern textbook says what that led to: armies of professional soldiers who owed more to their commander than to the state.

The two sentences are about the same year, 107 BCE, and they are different kinds of sentence. One comes from a man writing more than sixty years after the event and the other from a book written in our own time. How does a historian get from the first to the second, and how much weight can each carry?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell what an ancient writer reports from what a textbook concludes, and say which parts of the break between Roman soldiers and the Roman state rest on firm ground.
intro.whyItMatters: A textbook states conclusions the ancient writers never stated, and knowing which is which tells you how much each sentence can bear.

recap.keyIdea: The break between soldiers and the state rests firmly on events the sources report, such as the march on Rome, and much less firmly on the causes a textbook names.

blocks.text: Sallust reports two explanations for Marius enlisting the poor and does not choose between them, while the textbook states that the reforms led to client armies. The speech Sallust gives Marius shows Sallust's picture of the man, Plutarch's count of the lists rests on a reading of “as many”, and the dictatorship kept its old name while the gap of 120 years and the powers voted to Sulla mark it as something new.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to Catiline and the first triumvirate, and asks what to do when an author tells you he has no side.

lessons.title: Catiline, Cicero and the first triumvirate

lead.text: In 63 BCE a Roman aristocrat, Lucius Sergius Catilina, whom we call Catiline, was said to be at the head of a **conspiracy**: a secret plan by a group to seize power or overthrow the government. Sallust's *Conspiracy of Catiline* is the account we start from. He wrote it after Caesar was killed in 44 BCE, some twenty years after the events, and he was by then a man with a career behind him, as we are about to see.

The second account is Plutarch's. In his life of Cicero he tells of the Senate's debate on what to do with the conspirators, and Plutarch was born about the middle of the first century CE, more than a century after the debate. According to the outline of his life in the Loeb edition of the *Gallic War*, Caesar spoke in that debate, and he is the man both writers keep returning to.
Sallust gives his reason for writing, and with it a statement about himself.

reveal.text: The sentence tells us how Sallust wants to be read. The next screen sets it beside what is known of the man.

lead.text: J. C. Rolfe, in his introduction to the Loeb Classical Library edition of Sallust (1921), tells what is known of the man who made that promise. Sallust was tribune in 52 BCE and was expelled from the Senate by the censor in 50. Caesar reappointed him to a quaestorship in 49, which put him back in the Senate, and he was later made governor of Numidia and Africa as a reward for his services. After Caesar was assassinated he left public life and wrote history.

Rolfe adds that Sallust “professes complete impartiality”, that his leaning towards the popular party is “obvious”, and that it “has been suspected that he had the underlying motive of clearing Caesar” of any part in the plot. None of that proves he was partial in this book. It tells us where to look. A writer's statement that he has no interest in the matter is a **claimed impartiality**, and since it is itself something he chose to say, a historian tests it by reading what the book does.

Rolfe also finds a fault of dating. Sallust puts the beginning of the plot in 64 BCE when it was 63, which stretches a few months into more than a year and, in Rolfe's words, distorts the facts. An error of that kind says nothing about bias, but it is a warning against taking Sallust's sequence on trust.
Read how Sallust handles a story about Caesar.

reveal.text: In Sallust's telling the stories come from Caesar's enemies and fail with Cicero. That fits what Rolfe suspected about his purpose, and it is still a report of what was said.

lead.text: Plutarch gives the Senate's debate from another side. Catulus spoke first against Caesar's motion, and then Cato spoke so forcefully, bringing up the suspicion that hung over Caesar himself, that the Senate decreed the conspirators' execution. Caesar opposed the confiscation of their goods and, when many insisted, appealed to the tribunes, who would do nothing, until Cicero gave way.

Both writers, then, put suspicion of Caesar into the story. That looks like [[corroboration|Support for a claim from a second source that did not get it from the first. Met in “Hannibal in Italy and the numbers at Cannae”.]], but the word carries a condition. We do not know whether Plutarch used Sallust or some common earlier source, and if he did, the two are one witness repeated and not two. Until we know that, their agreement shows only that the suspicion was part of the story as it was told, and not that Caesar was involved.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the three possibilities. A historian can name the first two and has to say that the third is where we stand.

diagram.alt: Three diagrams of how Sallust and Plutarch might be connected. In the first, Plutarch copies Sallust, so there is one witness repeated. In the second, Plutarch has an earlier source of his own, so there are two witnesses. In the third, dashed arrows show that our sources do not say which.
diagram.caption: Two accounts of the same events count as two witnesses only if the second did not copy the first. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: The two passages are short, and a point that only one of them makes is not a contradiction.

reveal.text: Where the two overlap, they overlap on suspicion of Caesar and on Cicero's part in deciding. Each adds details the other lacks.

lead.text: In his life of Caesar Plutarch makes a claim about causes. Most people, he says, blame the quarrel between Pompey and Caesar for the civil wars, but he puts the origin earlier, in their partnership, when they first worked together against the aristocracy and only later fell out with each other.

The union he means is the **triumvirate** of 60 BCE: a private alliance of three men, Pompey, Crassus and Caesar. Caesar was consul in 59 BCE, his command in Gaul began in 58 BCE, Crassus was killed fighting the Parthians at Carrhae in 53 BCE, and Caesar crossed the Rubicon in January 49 BCE. The textbook agrees on 60 BCE and on the Rubicon. A claim about a cause is tested by asking what else would be true if it were right, and the first thing to ask here is how long the alliance lasted before the war it is said to have begun.

diagram.caption: The alliance of 60 BCE and the Rubicon of 49 BCE. The second view shows the stretch between them.

lead.text: Find the interval, using the dates on the timeline.

reveal.text: That interval is long, which does not make Plutarch wrong. It means that his claim needs more than the two dates.

lead.text: Plutarch's sentence is a claim about a cause, and a claim of that kind can be strengthened in several ways.

reveal.text: The strongest support would be something the alliance did before the quarrel began. A repeat of the sentence, or a fact that both sides accept, leaves the claim where it was.

steps.headline: A law, a description and an accusation

lead.text: One rule can reach us in three forms. Table IX of the Twelve Tables, traditionally dated to about 450 BCE, forbids the killing of any man who has not been convicted, whoever he may be. Polybius, a Greek historian who lived about 200 to 118 BCE, describes the people as the one court that decides cases of life and death. Plutarch tells that after Cicero's consulship Caesar declared in a public assembly that Lentulus, Cethegus and their accomplices had been executed without a trial and so without proper legal process, and that this was the charge brought against Cicero.

Each is a different kind of evidence about the same rule. The law says what Rome's own rule was meant to be, the description shows how an outside observer understood the courts to work, and the accusation shows someone using the rule against a man in a later crisis. None of them settles whether the executions were illegal, and the passages give no verdict, but together they show what Cicero's critics were pointing at.

lessons.orientation: Treat Sallust's claim of impartiality as something to test, say when Plutarch's account supports his, and judge Plutarch's claim about why the civil wars began.

lessons.nextAction: Read Caesar's own reports of his campaigns for who each explanation is written for, and compare them with Plutarch.

blocks.text: Sallust opens his account of Catiline's plot by saying that no hope, fear or party loyalty bent his judgment. It is a reassuring thing for a writer to say, and it is also a sentence that Sallust chose to put there, in a book about a plot against Rome in 63 BCE and about the men, Caesar among them, who were suspected of having a hand in it.
Plutarch tells part of the same story more than a century later. How would you test a writer's claim about himself, and what does it take for a second account to count as support?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to treat a writer's claim of impartiality as something to test, say when two accounts support each other, and judge a claim about why a war began.
intro.whyItMatters: Writers tell you about their own motives, and ancient accounts often repeat one another, so you need ways to test both before you rely on them.

recap.keyIdea: A writer's claim to be impartial is a claim to test against his career and his book, and two accounts that agree count as support only if the second did not copy the first.

blocks.text: Sallust says his mind was free of hope, fear and partisanship, yet Rolfe describes a man who served Caesar, leans towards the popular party, may have meant to clear Caesar of the plot, and dated the plot a year too early. Plutarch also puts suspicion on Caesar, but we cannot tell whether he drew on Sallust. His claim that the union of Pompey, Crassus and Caesar began the civil wars is a claim about cause, and it needs evidence of what the union did in the eleven years before the Rubicon.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson reads Caesar's own reports of his campaigns, and asks who each of his explanations is written for.

lessons.title: Caesar in his own words and in Plutarch's

lead.text: Caesar (100 to 44 BCE) wrote two accounts of his wars, and in both he refers to himself as “Caesar” and “he”. Each is a **commentary**: his own report of his campaigns, written in the third person for readers at Rome. The *Gallic War* covers the campaigns he fought in Gaul from 58 BCE onwards, and some scholars hold that its first seven books were written in the winter of 52 to 51 BCE and published early in 51, though the Loeb introduction says that how and when it appeared is an open question. The *Civil War* covers the war that began in 49 BCE, and Caesar left it unfinished when he died.

The same introduction suggests why the *Gallic War* would have been valuable to him at that moment: as “a vindication to the Senate of his campaigns and conquests”. That makes Caesar an unusual witness. He was there, and he knew what he did and ordered, and he is also the man whose conduct his readers were judging. Plutarch, who wrote about a century after Caesar's death, was in the opposite position, because he was far from the events and had no stake in them.

afterFigure.text: So each has something to offer. Caesar's commentaries are the nearest evidence we have for the campaigns, and the account Caesar most wanted believed. Plutarch's life adds scenes and thoughts that Caesar never wrote.

diagram.alt: A timeline of Caesar's years from 58 to 44 BCE with the Helvetian campaign, the Gallic War possibly published in 51, the Rubicon in 49, Pharsalus in 48 and Caesar's death in 44. A second view shows a gap of about a century between Caesar's death and Plutarch's birth about 50 CE.

lead.text: Here is how Caesar explains his march into Gaul, in a sentence he writes about himself.

reveal.text: A reason for a war is chosen with its readers in mind. The next screen gives that kind of reason a name.

lead.text: A reason that a writer gives for an action, chosen to persuade, is a **justification**. Caesar's reason for going to Gaul is one. He says that the Helvetii intended to march through the lands of the Sequani and the Aedui towards the territory of the Santones, near a state in the Province, and that “if this took place” there would be great danger to the Province.

Look at how the reason is built. The Helvetii “intend” to march, and Caesar has been told so: the sentence before the one in the extract says, in the passive, that Caesar was told again of the Helvetii's plan, without saying who told him. The danger is a prediction, “if this took place”, so nothing that actually happened could test it. None of this makes the reason false. It does mean that a historian cannot treat it as a record of events, because it is Caesar's account of what he was told and what he judged.
Compare Sallust on Marius, whose two reasons were things said by others and reported with a hedge. Caesar's is an argument that he makes himself, in a calm voice and without a hedge.

Caesar gives numbers. In the camp of the Helvetii, he says, lists turned up that were written in Greek letters, that counted those who had set out from their country, those able to bear arms, and, separately, the children, the elderly and the women. He reports five groups: 263,000 Helvetii, 36,000 Tulingi, 14,000 Latobrigi, 23,000 Rauraci and 32,000 Boii, a total of 368,000, of whom about 92,000 could bear arms. He adds that a census of those who went home, taken at his command, found 110,000.

Each of these is a **count and census**: a figure Caesar gives from a list or a count, where the question is who made it. The Helvetii made the lists, and Caesar ordered the census of those at home. We learn of both only through his book, so the numbers pass through the man whose war it was, and nobody outside his camp reports them.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the five groups to scale and then sets the total beside the number counted at home.

steps.headline: Check that Caesar's five lists add up to his total.

workedSteps.text: Add the first two lists, the Helvetii and the Tulingi.
Add the Latobrigi.
Add the Rauraci.
Add the Boii, and compare the result with the total Caesar reports.

lead.text: Use his figures as they stand.

reveal.text: The result of 258,000 is a historian's subtraction. Caesar does not say what became of those people, and the census that gives the 110,000 was taken at his order.

lead.text: Plutarch gives totals as well. In his life of Caesar he says that in less than ten years in Gaul Caesar took more than eight hundred towns by storm, subdued three hundred states, and fought three million men, of whom he killed one million and took a second million captive.

Those are totals for the whole of the Gallic wars, and they are Plutarch's, not Caesar's. Plutarch states them flatly and does not say whose count they come from, whereas Caesar's census of one migration comes with an account of who made it. A historian asks of a number what it counts and who counted it, which is the question of its [[authority|The earlier writer a historian names as the source of a claim. Met in “Hannibal in Italy and the numbers at Cannae”.]]. On both questions the two figures differ, and the answers show why the larger one is the harder to use.
The two numbers are not about the same thing.

reveal.text: Plutarch's figure spans years of war and Caesar's one migration in one year, so a historian can use each for its own question and cannot subtract one from the other.

lead.text: At the start of the civil war Caesar reports a speech to his soldiers. He says he complained that the tribunes' right of intercession, which Sulla had given back only a few years earlier, was being treated as a crime and put down by force, and that Sulla, who had taken every other power from the tribunes, had still left that one alone. He added that the Senate's decree telling the magistrates to see that the republic came to no harm had been used only when dangerous laws were proposed, when tribunes tried violent measures, or when the people seceded, and that those cases had been paid for by the deaths of Saturninus and the Gracchi. Nothing of that kind, he said, was happening now.

Sulla, the Gracchi and the [[secession|A refusal by the plebeians to serve or to stay in the city until their demands were met. Met in “The Struggle of the Orders and the Twelve Tables”.]] of the plebeians are the Roman past that you have been reading. Caesar picks from it the precedents that suit him, and the soldiers of the thirteenth legion, he says, shouted that they would defend their general and the tribunes. A justification of this kind is an argument from history, and a historian is entitled to check each precedent against what the other sources say about it.
Read part of the speech as Caesar gives it.

reveal.text: Sulla and Pompey appear in the speech as men who changed the tribunes' powers. That is Caesar's account of them, put to work in his own cause.

lead.text: The most famous scene of the civil war is not in Caesar's book. In the part of the *Civil War* we have, the first book, he never names the Rubicon at all. The scene is Plutarch's. He has Caesar come to the river that divides Gaul from the rest of Italy and halt, wavering, and change his mind first one way and then the other, without a word to anyone. At last, in a sort of passion, he uses the proverb “The die is cast” and crosses. The textbook dates the crossing to January 49 BCE.

How could Plutarch know what a man thought while he said nothing? He gives one clue: the friends with Caesar included Asinius Pollio. Elsewhere in the same life Plutarch cites Pollio by name for words Caesar spoke at Pharsalus, so Pollio may have been a source for him. For the Rubicon, though, Plutarch does not say so. The name gives a historian a lead and does not settle anything, and the scene stays a later writer's picture of Caesar's mind.
Look at what Plutarch says about who was with Caesar.

reveal.text: A name in a later account is a clue and not a proof. The next step for a historian would be to look for what Pollio himself wrote, and for what other writers took from it.

lessons.orientation: Read Caesar's own reports of Gaul and the civil war for who each explanation is written for, check a number he gives, and say what Plutarch's later scenes add.
lessons.reviewLabel: Caesar in his own words and in Plutarch's
lessons.nextAction: Test Augustus's own list of his deeds against Plutarch and the textbook, and say what changed and what stayed after 27 BCE.

blocks.text: Caesar explains why he went to war in Gaul in a single sentence, and he writes it about himself in the third person: that warlike men who were enemies of the Roman people would, if they settled beside an open and very fertile stretch of country, be a great danger to the Province. The voice is calm and impersonal, like an official report.

Plutarch tells much of the same career more than a century later, with scenes and thoughts that Caesar never wrote. What can a historian take from a general's own report of his own war, and what from a biographer who came long after?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a general's report of his own war for who it was written for, check a number he gives, and say what a later biographer adds.
intro.whyItMatters: A general's account is the nearest evidence we have for his campaigns and also the account he most wanted believed, so it has to be read for both.

recap.keyIdea: A general's own report is the nearest evidence for his campaigns and also the account he most wanted believed, so a historian asks who each explanation is written for and who made each number.

blocks.text: Caesar gives his reasons for war in the third person for readers at Rome, reports lists and a census that only his book describes, and tells his soldiers a history made of precedents. Plutarch's totals count the whole of the Gallic wars and cannot be set against Caesar's count of one migration, and his scene at the Rubicon is a picture of thoughts that Caesar's own pages never describe. Each source answers some questions well and others poorly.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson reads Augustus's own list of his deeds and tests it against what Plutarch says and what the list leaves out.

lessons.title: Augustus: the Republic restored, in his own words

steps.headline: A list set up in public

lead.text: The **Res Gestae** is Augustus's own list of what he had done, and in the first-person voice it uses it reads like a speech cut in stone. In the Loeb introduction F. W. Shipley explains how it survives. Augustus left it among his papers with the Vestal Virgins, with instructions that “a résumé of his acts” be engraved on bronze tablets before his mausoleum, and it was also copied on the walls of temples of Augustus across the empire. The copy we have comes from the temple at Ancyra in Asia Minor, which Shipley calls the modern Angora, and it carries a Greek version beside the Latin.

Shipley adds two cautions. The text was begun long before 14 CE, the year Augustus died, and was added to from time to time. And it is written with “studied objectivity”, in which “everything of a personal nature is omitted” and the story is limited to his dealings with the Senate and the people. It is the one source in this course in which the ruler himself speaks.
Here is the first sentence of the list, as it was displayed.

reveal.text: Display tells us that Augustus cared how the sentence would be read. What a reader should do with it is the next question.

lead.text: In the second chapter Augustus says of the men who killed Julius Caesar, his adoptive father, that he drove them into exile and punished their deed by lawful process, and that when they went to war on the republic he twice defeated them in battle. Plutarch tells another side of those years. After the assassination, he says, the young man, once consul, made peace with Antony and Lepidus, joined his power to theirs and shared out the government with them like a piece of property. Together they drew up a list of more than two hundred people to be put to death, met for three days near Bononia and fought hardest over Cicero's case, and on the third day the young Caesar, as Plutarch calls him, gave way and surrendered Cicero. Plutarch prefaces Caesar's pleading for Cicero with “it is said”, a hedge worth noticing.

The Res Gestae has no list and no Cicero: a word search of the translation finds neither. A silence like that has at least two readings, and the [[silence|The absence of a voice or a topic in the record, which can be a fact about the past or only about the evidence. Met in “Silences, survival and one-sided records”.]] rule from the History course applies: it does not show that nothing happened. A list of achievements is not expected to hold everything, and Shipley says that this one leaves out whatever is personal. The silence also suits a man who wants to be remembered a certain way, and so it is a reason to look at other sources, and here Plutarch is the one we have.

The other sources are few, as the figure shows. Between Caesar's death in 44 BCE and Actium in 31 BCE, the sources this course has are Plutarch's life of Cicero, which covers the year 43, the textbook's summary and Augustus himself. There is no account from Antony's side. Where the sources are this few, a historian says how few they are and does not fill the gap from memory.

The second view marks the years from 44 to 31 and lists the three sources this course has for them.

lead.text: Set the two accounts side by side.

reveal.text: Plutarch's list and Augustus's silence do not cancel each other. Together they tell a historian where the record is thin and where to look next.

lead.text: Augustus says the dictatorship was offered to him by the people and the Senate, in his absence and later when he was present, in the consulship of Marcus Marcellus and Lucius Arruntius, and that he did not accept it. What he did accept, he says, was the charge of the grain supply at a time of great scarcity, which he administered so that within a few days he freed the whole people, at his own expense, from fear and danger. The textbook says that in 27 BCE Octavian formally gave up his dictatorial powers and, in its word, restored the Republic.

These cannot both be true, since a man cannot step down from an office that he refused. A historian might be tempted to settle it by type: the Res Gestae is a primary source and the textbook a secondary one. But Augustus has a reason to say he refused, because it fits the story that he restored the Republic, and the textbook gives no source for its sentence. One difference helps. Augustus names the year in which it was offered, by its consuls, so a historian can test that against records of the year, while the textbook gives only 27 BCE and says no more. The pack has no third source, so this lesson cannot settle the point. It can say how a historian would go about it.
Treat the disagreement as a historian would.

reveal.text: Neither side wins by being older, newer or more confident. What settles a conflict between a self-account and a summary is a third source.

lead.text: Augustus says he handed the republic from his own control back to the Senate and people, that he was given the title Augustus by decree, and that after that time he stood above everyone in rank but held no more power than his colleagues in any magistracy. The textbook tells it differently. After he had filled the Senate with his supporters, it says, the Senate appointed him proconsul of the frontier provinces, which made him in effect commander of the whole army, honoured him as leader of the Senate and gave him the title Augustus. In 23 BCE it gave him several powers of a tribune, including a veto over officials, the Senate and the assemblies.

The textbook calls the result a **facade**: an outward form kept after the substance has changed. The system takes its name from the title the Senate gave him, *Princeps Senatus*, and is called the **principate**: a system in which a first citizen held power through the old offices. The table sets what Polybius described, in the second lesson, beside what the textbook says of Augustus, one pair of rows at a time.

afterFigure.text: Read the shaded cells for what the textbook says moved. Consuls and assemblies continued in form. The Senate, the tribunes' veto and the command of the army are where, in the textbook's account, one man gathered the power.

The cells for the Senate, tribunes and army are shaded where the textbook says power moved to Augustus.

steps.headline: Work out how many years passed from the settlement of 27 BCE to Augustus's death in 14 CE.

workedSteps.text: Years BCE count down towards 1 BCE and years CE count up from 1 CE, and no year numbered 0 lies between them.
From 27 BCE to 1 BCE is 26 years.
From 1 BCE to 1 CE is one more year.
From 1 CE to 14 CE is 13 more years.
The short way is to add the two year numbers and take one off, which gives the same 40 years.

lead.text: Augustus counts the thirty-seventh year of his tribunician power at the time of writing. Use the textbook's date for its start.

reveal.text: Counting 23 BCE as the first year, 14 CE is the thirty-seventh, which is how Augustus's own count fits the 36 years that passed.

lead.text: Apply what the table shows to the settlement as a whole.

reveal.text: Both the Res Gestae and the textbook are partly right. Augustus did keep the offices, and the textbook is right that the powers behind them had gathered in one man.

lessons.orientation: Test Augustus's own account of his career against Plutarch and the textbook, and say what changed and what stayed in the constitution after 27 BCE.
lessons.reviewLabel: Augustus: the Republic restored, in his own words
lessons.nextAction: You can now read an ancient writer for his purpose, check a number or a claim against another source, and say what changed and what stayed.

blocks.text: Augustus's own list of his deeds opens with a sentence about him at the age of nineteen, in which he says he raised an army on his own initiative and at his own expense and used it to set the republic free from the tyranny of a faction. The document was cut in stone and copied on temple walls across the empire, so anyone who passed could read it.

Here the checks on it are a biographer who wrote long afterwards and a textbook, and between 44 and 31 BCE the sources are thinner still. How do you test a ruler's account of himself, and what do you say when the checks run out?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to test a ruler's account of himself against later sources, say what a silence in it may mean, and describe what changed and what stayed under Augustus.
intro.whyItMatters: A ruler's own account is the easiest to quote and the hardest to check, so it matters where you can test it and where you cannot.

recap.keyIdea: A ruler's own account is evidence of how he wanted to be remembered, so a historian tests it against other sources, notes what it leaves out, and says plainly where the checks run out.

blocks.text: The Res Gestae was set up in public and is silent about the lists Plutarch describes, a silence that marks a point to check and does not prove the lists happened. On the dictatorship Augustus and the textbook disagree, and only a third source could settle it. After 27 BCE the consuls and the Senate still met, and the textbook's account is that the power behind them moved to one man, which is what the word facade names.

questions.prompt: Livy says this in his preface. What does it tell a reader about how to use his story of Romulus?

extracts.text: The traditions which have come down to us of what happened before the building of the city, or before its building was contemplated, as being suitable rather to the fictions of poetry than to the genuine records of history, I have no intention either to affirm or refute.
extracts.who: Livy, History of Rome (Spillan translation)
extracts.when: preface to the first book, written from about 28 BCE
extracts.kind: A historian's statement of how he will treat the stories of the founding

hints: Look at the two verbs he uses about the traditions. Is either one 'confirm'?
Livy goes on to tell the stories. What would that do if he were refusing them altogether?

acceptedIdeas: Treat it as a tradition he passes on, not one he guarantees
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Treat it as a tradition he passes on, not one he guarantees

questions.onCorrect: Livy keeps the tales in his book and withholds his guarantee, so a reader uses them as traditions and looks for evidence elsewhere.

misconceptions.feedback: He says the stories belong to poetry as much as to history and that he will not affirm them, which is the opposite of saying he checked them.
A tradition can still show how Romans told their beginnings. Livy keeps the stories in his book, so the sensible move is to use them for what they show.

choices.label: Treat it as a tradition he passes on, not one he guarantees
Treat it as a record he has checked against documents
Leave it out, because a legend is worth nothing as evidence

questions.prompt: This is Livy's scene of the death of Lucretia, whose wrong at the hands of the king's son set off the end of the monarchy. What is the scene best evidence of?

extracts.text: "It is for you to see," says she, "what is due to him. As for me, though I acquit myself of guilt, from punishment I do not discharge myself; nor shall any woman survive her dishonour pleading the example of Lucretia." The knife, which she kept concealed beneath her garment, she plunges into her heart, and falling forward on the wound, she dropped down expiring.
extracts.who: Livy, History of Rome (Spillan translation)
extracts.when: begun about 28 BCE, nearly five centuries after the events it tells
extracts.kind: A history of Rome written for Roman readers

hints: Count the years between the date the scene is set and the date Livy began writing.
What did Livy's readers expect of a good Roman woman, and how does the scene meet that?

acceptedIdeas: How a Roman of Livy's day told the end of the kings
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How a Roman of Livy's day told the end of the kings

questions.onCorrect: A scene composed centuries later shows what its writer thought worth telling, here honour, an oath and the cost of tyranny.

misconceptions.feedback: Nobody recorded the event when it happened. Livy wrote nearly five centuries later, and the words he gives Lucretia are his.
The scene is a story about a wrong and an oath. It names no office and gives no list of magistrates.

choices.label: What the king's son said and did in 509 BCE, word for word
How a Roman of Livy's day told the end of the kings
Who held office in the first year of the new Republic

questions.prompt: The extract is Livy's account of the change from kings to consuls. A modern textbook adds that historians read the story of the expulsion of the Tarquins as loosely based on real events, in which the city freed itself from Etruscan rule and became an independent republic around 500 BCE. What does the textbook add that Livy's sentence does not?

extracts.text: But the origin of liberty you may date from this period, rather because the consular authority was made annual, than that any diminution was made from the kingly prerogative. The first consuls had all their privileges and ensigns of authority, only care was taken that the terror might not appear doubled, by both having the fasces at the same time.
extracts.who: Livy, History of Rome (Spillan translation)
extracts.when: begun about 28 BCE, nearly five centuries after the events it describes
extracts.kind: A history of Rome written for Roman readers

hints: Livy's sentence tells what changed. Does the textbook tell what changed, or why it might have?
Look at the Etruscan rule the textbook mentions. Does Livy's sentence mention it?

acceptedIdeas: A wider setting that might explain the change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A wider setting that might explain the change

questions.onCorrect: Livy says what changed in the consulship, and the textbook puts that change inside Rome freeing itself from Etruscan rule.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither account offers a record made in 509 BCE. The textbook in fact gives only 'around 500 BCE'.
The textbook doubts the details of the expulsion story, not the change itself. It says the story is loosely based on real events.

choices.label: A wider setting that might explain the change
A date for the change that was recorded at the time
A reason to doubt that Rome ever had any consuls

questions.prompt: On the traditional dates of 753 BCE for the founding and 509 BCE for the end of the kings, how many years did the kings rule?
hints: Both dates are BCE, so the earlier one has the larger number.
Subtract the later date from the earlier one.
Take 509 away from 753 and write down the difference.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both dates are BCE, so the years count down and the gap is 753 minus 509, which is 244.

questions.onCorrect: The kings ruled 244 years on the tradition's own dates, and nothing in the figure was recorded at the time.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two dates. Both count down from the same point, so subtract them.

questions.prompt: Livy's summary gives the last three kings 38, 40 and 25 years. Of the 244 years, how many are left for the first four kings?
hints: Add the three reigns Livy gives first.
The kings together ruled 244 years on the traditional dates.
Take the sum of the three reigns away from 244.
questions.onCorrect: The first four kings share 141 years, a figure that comes from the tradition's dates and has no record of its own.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the last three reigns. The question asks for what is left of the 244 years.
That adds 244 and 103. The last three reigns are part of the 244 years, so take them away.

questions.prompt: A historian lists five things that bear on the early city of Rome. Which are stories told later, and which were found in the ground?
hints: Ask of each item whether someone wrote it down or someone dug it up.
A list can still be a tradition. Ask who made it, and when.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The she-wolf tale, the Lucretia scene and the list of kings are stories told later. The wall and the Greek pottery are finds.

questions.onCorrect: Stories and finds can concern the same hill, and each is read by asking who made it and when.

items.label: The she-wolf and the twins, as Livy tells it
items.explanation: It is a tale handed down and written by Livy long after, and he reports it as a tradition.

items.label: Lucretia's oath and death, as Livy tells it
items.explanation: It is a scene Livy composed from the tradition, not a record made at the time.

items.label: Livy's list of seven kings and their reigns
items.explanation: The list is a tradition too, set down by Livy, and it has no record of its own beside it.

items.label: A wall found around the Palatine Hill in 1988
items.explanation: It was found in the ground, so it is a thing left by the time itself.

items.label: Greek pottery found on the Palatine Hill
items.explanation: Pottery was found at the place, and the textbook reads it as a sign that trade took place.

questions.prompt: Livy has just told how a she-wolf found the twin founders and nursed them. He then adds this sentence. What does it show about how he handles the tale?

extracts.text: Some are of opinion that she was called Lupa among the shepherds, from her being a common prostitute, and that this gave rise to the surprising story.
extracts.who: Livy, History of Rome (Spillan translation)
extracts.when: begun about 28 BCE, nearly five centuries after the events it tells
extracts.kind: A history of Rome written for Roman readers

hints: What does 'some are of opinion' do to the claim that follows?
Is the tale still in Livy's book, or has he left it out?

acceptedIdeas: He passes the tale on and notes a plain explanation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: He passes the tale on and notes a plain explanation

questions.onCorrect: Hedges such as 'some are of opinion' mark a writer who is passing something on, and the reader treats the tale the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: The sentence offers a plain explanation for the wolf. It gives no record, and nothing in it confirms the tale.
He keeps the tale in his book. He reports the explanation as what some people think, not as a proof.

choices.label: He has checked the tale against a record and found it true
He drops the tale, because the explanation proves it false
He passes the tale on and notes a plain explanation

questions.prompt: What is the word for a story handed down about the past without a record made at the time?
hints: The word is also used for the founding stories of Rome.
It is the word Livy's own preface is about.

acceptedIdeas: tradition
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: tradition

questions.onCorrect: A tradition can be old and well loved and still lack any record made when the events happened.

questions.prompt: Roman tradition gives 509 BCE for the expulsion of the Tarquins, and a modern textbook places the events behind the story around 500 BCE. Why does the textbook give a round date?
hints: Is there a record that fixes the year?
The textbook calls the story only loosely based on real events. What does that do to the claim?

acceptedIdeas: The tradition's 509 is a date no record can confirm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tradition's 509 is a date no record can confirm

questions.onCorrect: A rounded date is an honest answer when the year itself came from a tradition and no record can fix it.

misconceptions.feedback: The textbook points to no new record. It only says that the event happened around that time.
A small gap does not make the other dates sound. None of them was recorded when the events happened.

choices.label: A record has now been found that moves the event to 500 BCE
The tradition's 509 is a date no record can confirm
The tradition is wrong by nine years, so its other dates are sound

questions.prompt: Polybius's first plan for the Histories ran from 220 BCE to 168 BCE. How many years is that?

extracts.text: in what manner, and under what kind of constitution, it came about that nearly the whole world fell under the power of Rome in somewhat less than fifty-three years,—an event certainly without precedent.
extracts.who: Polybius, Histories, book 6 (Shuckburgh translation)
extracts.when: by a Greek (about 200 to about 118 BCE) describing Rome at Cannae, 216 BCE
extracts.kind: A Greek historian's account of Rome's constitution, written for Greek readers

hints: Both dates are BCE, so the earlier year has the larger number.
Subtract 168 from 220.
Compare your answer with his phrase 'somewhat less than fifty-three years'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both dates are BCE, so subtract the later year from the earlier: 220 minus 168 is 52.

questions.onCorrect: The span comes to 52 years, which is why Polybius calls it somewhat less than fifty-three, a number chosen to stress how fast Rome rose.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts both end years. The distance from 168 BCE to 220 BCE is a plain subtraction.
That adds the two years. Both count down from the same point, so subtract them.

questions.prompt: In Polybius's account, which body controlled the treasury, so that public money was paid out only on its decree?
hints: Polybius gives each body a few main powers. Which one does he link to money?
Who has to issue a decree before the quaestors pay anyone?

acceptedIdeas: The Senate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Senate

questions.onCorrect: Polybius says the Senate regulated receipts and payments alike, which is the root of its hold over the other two.

misconceptions.feedback: A consul on campaign could draw on the treasury, but Polybius says the quaestors cannot issue money without a Senate decree except for the consuls' service, and the legions' supplies still need one.
The people ratified treaties and passed laws, as Polybius says. The treasury was not among its powers.

choices.label: The Senate
The consuls
The assembly of the people

questions.prompt: Here are six powers that Polybius describes. Which body holds each of them in his account?
hints: Ask first who does the thing, then ask who has to agree before it stands.
Two bodies have two items each and two have one.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Consuls summon the meetings and introduce ambassadors, the Senate controls the treasury, the people ratify treaties and pass laws, and a tribune can stop the Senate.

questions.onCorrect: Most powers in Polybius's account belong to one body and are limited by another, which is the point of calling the system mixed.

items.label: Summon the popular meetings and put proposals to them
items.explanation: Polybius says it is the consuls' business to summon the meetings, bring proposals forward and carry out the majority's decrees.

items.label: Introduce foreign ambassadors to the Senate
items.explanation: The consuls bring ambassadors in and put matters before the Senate.

items.label: Control the treasury through decrees to the quaestors
items.explanation: No public money is issued without a Senate decree, except for the consuls' service.

items.label: Ratify or refuse a treaty
items.explanation: Provisional terms of alliance or peace stand only if the people ratify them.

items.label: Pass or repeal a law
items.explanation: Polybius gives the people absolute power of passing or repealing laws.

items.label: Stop the Senate from passing a decree or even meeting
items.explanation: A tribune who interposes a veto leaves the Senate unable to decree or to meet.

questions.prompt: Polybius says the people decide on war and ratify treaties. The textbook adds that in the assembly able to declare war, wealthier citizens had more votes. What does that add?
hints: Is Polybius or the textbook the one who gives detail about how votes were counted?
Does the textbook say the people had no part, or that some votes weighed more?

acceptedIdeas: His 'people' hides that votes were weighted by wealth
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: His 'people' hides that votes were weighted by wealth

questions.onCorrect: A source can be accurate about a power and still skip how it was shared, and a second source can show the gap.

misconceptions.feedback: The textbook says the opposite. In that assembly the blocs of wealthier citizens carried more votes, and nobody in the passage disputes that.
The textbook agrees that the assembly could declare war. It qualifies who had most weight in it, and does not remove the people's part.

choices.label: Every citizen's vote counted the same, so the textbook corrects him
His 'people' hides that votes were weighted by wealth
The people had no say, so Polybius is simply wrong

questions.prompt: The textbook also says the Senate controlled public spending, though it does not say where it got this. Does that agreement settle that Polybius is right?
hints: Ask whether the textbook had a way to know this other than reading someone like Polybius.
What did the History course say makes agreement count as corroboration?

acceptedIdeas: It supports him, but the two may not be independent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It supports him, but the two may not be independent

questions.onCorrect: Two sources agree more convincingly when each had its own route to the fact.

misconceptions.feedback: Agreement counts as corroboration only when the sources reached the fact separately. A textbook may simply rest on writers such as Polybius.
A modern writer can add real weight, for instance from inscriptions or other writers. The trouble here is that this one gives no source of its own.

choices.label: Yes, two sources agree, so the claim is settled
No, a modern textbook can never confirm an ancient writer
It supports him, but the two may not be independent

questions.prompt: Polybius was a Greek explaining why Rome rose so fast. Which is the best reason to check his account of the Senate against another source?

extracts.text: in what manner, and under what kind of constitution, it came about that nearly the whole world fell under the power of Rome in somewhat less than fifty-three years,—an event certainly without precedent.
extracts.who: Polybius, Histories, book 6 (Shuckburgh translation)
extracts.when: by a Greek (about 200 to about 118 BCE) describing Rome at Cannae, 216 BCE
extracts.kind: A Greek historian's account of Rome's constitution, written for Greek readers

hints: Look at what he says the work will let readers 'know and fully realise'.
What would a writer with that aim want his description of the system to show?

acceptedIdeas: He is explaining Rome's success, so he tends to find it well balanced
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: He is explaining Rome's success, so he tends to find it well balanced

questions.onCorrect: A writer who wants to prove the constitution caused the success has a reason to describe it as well balanced.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the extract suggests invention. The reason to check him is his purpose, not a guess about what he could read.
That sweeps in every Greek writer without evidence. Polybius is worth weighing for his own purpose, which the extract states.

choices.label: He could not read Latin, so he invented many of his details
He is explaining Rome's success, so he tends to find it well balanced
Greek writers never described Roman institutions with accuracy

questions.prompt: What is the word for a tribune's power to stop an act by saying 'I forbid'?
hints: It is the Latin word for 'I forbid'.
The Senate could not even hold a meeting if a tribune used it.

acceptedIdeas: veto
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: veto

questions.onCorrect: A tribune who used the veto could keep the Senate from passing a decree or even meeting.

questions.prompt: Polybius says this about the three bodies. What does he conclude from the fact that each, taken alone, looks like a different system?

extracts.text: And no wonder: for if we confine our observation to the power of the Consuls we should be inclined to regard it as despotic; if on that of the Senate, as aristocratic; and if finally one looks at the power possessed by the people it would seem a clear case of a democracy.
extracts.who: Polybius, Histories, book 6 (Shuckburgh translation)
extracts.when: by a Greek (about 200 to about 118 BCE) describing Rome at Cannae, 216 BCE
extracts.kind: A Greek historian's account of Rome's constitution, written for Greek readers

hints: Count how many of the three bodies he describes as looking like a different system.
Does he say any one body wins?

acceptedIdeas: No one name fits it, since it mixes all three kinds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No one name fits it, since it mixes all three kinds

questions.onCorrect: Polybius's view is that the three elements are balanced, so each of the three single labels fits only part of the whole.

misconceptions.feedback: The consul's power is only one of the three he lists, and he goes on to show it depends on the Senate and the people.
He argues that a consul needs both bodies' support, so the opposite holds.

choices.label: Rome was in all but name a monarchy under its consuls
The consuls could overrule the Senate and the people alike
No one name fits it, since it mixes all three kinds

questions.prompt: Source A is Livy's veteran describing how debt cost him his land and his freedom. Source B is a clause of Rome's first written law code on debt. What is the best use of the two together?

extracts.text: that this debt, aggravated by usury, had stripped him first of his father's and grandfather's farm, then of his other property; lastly that a pestilence, as it were, had reached his person. That he was taken by his creditor, not into servitude, but into a house of correction and a place of execution.
extracts.who: Livy, History of Rome (Spillan translation)
extracts.when: begun about 28 BCE, more than four centuries after the events it describes
extracts.kind: A history of Rome written for Roman readers

extracts.text: Unless he pays the amount of the judgment or some one in the presence of the magistrate interferes in his behalf as protector the creditor so shall take him home and fasten him in stocks or fetters. He shall fasten him with not less than fifteen pounds of weight or, if he choose, with more.
extracts.who: The Twelve Tables (Thatcher translation, 1901), Table III
extracts.when: traditionally dated to about 450 BCE and known today only in fragments
extracts.kind: Rome's first written laws, published in the Forum

hints: Ask what each source was made to do. A law lays down a rule, and a story makes a reader feel something.
Livy began writing more than four centuries after the Tables. What can he know about one man's debt?

acceptedIdeas: The law shows what was allowed, and the scene shows how the harm was pictured
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The law shows what was allowed, and the scene shows how the harm was pictured

questions.onCorrect: A law shows what someone meant to allow, and a later narrative shows how its author wanted the harm to be felt.

misconceptions.feedback: A rule says what was allowed, and a scene written centuries later says nothing about how often it happened. Neither source is a count of cases.
The scene is weak evidence of the event and still real evidence of how Livy's Romans pictured a debtor's grievance.

choices.label: The law shows what was allowed, and the scene shows how the harm was pictured
The scene proves that the law was always applied as harshly as this
The law is the only reliable source, so the scene can safely be ignored

questions.prompt: This is a clause of the Twelve Tables. What is it best evidence of?

extracts.text: Table XI. 1. Marriages should not take place between plebeians and patricians.
extracts.who: The Twelve Tables (Thatcher translation, 1901)
extracts.when: traditionally dated to about 450 BCE and known today only in fragments
extracts.kind: Rome's first written laws, published in the Forum

hints: A rule is evidence of what someone wanted. What did the people who wrote this want?
Does the clause say anything about the years after it was written?

acceptedIdeas: That the two orders were treated as legally apart
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the two orders were treated as legally apart

questions.onCorrect: A clause that forbids something shows that it was a concern of the lawmakers, though not how often it happened.

misconceptions.feedback: A ban shows that someone wanted the practice stopped. It leaves open whether any such marriage had taken place.
The clause is a single moment in the code. It says nothing about when, or whether, the ban was ever lifted.

choices.label: That no plebeian had ever married a patrician before this
That the two orders were treated as legally apart
That the ban stayed in force through the whole Struggle

questions.prompt: The plebeian consul was required from 367 BCE, and the laws of the plebeian assembly bound all citizens from 287 BCE. How many years is that?
hints: Both years are BCE, so the earlier one has the larger number.
Subtract 287 from 367.
Check that your answer is smaller than the gap from 450 BCE to 287 BCE.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both dates are BCE, so subtract the later from the earlier: 367 minus 287 is 80.

questions.onCorrect: The Struggle's later steps came across eighty years, long after the first written laws.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two years. They count down from the same point, so subtract them.

questions.prompt: Here are six statements about the early Republic. Which describe something that changed, and which something that stayed the same?
hints: Ask whether the statement describes how things were before and after, or whether it describes something that carried on.
Three statements on each side.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Written laws, the plebeian consul and binding plebeian laws are changes. The kinds of governing body, the limit of the equality won and the Tables' standing in law are what stayed.

items.label: Rome's laws were written down and open to all citizens

items.label: One of the two consuls had to be a plebeian, after 367 BCE
items.explanation: The highest office had been closed to plebeians, and the rule opened one of its two places.

items.label: Laws of the plebeian assembly bound all citizens, after 287 BCE
items.explanation: Plebeians now had a way to make law that bound every citizen.

items.label: Rome was still governed by elected magistrates, a Senate and assemblies
items.explanation: The textbook describes the same kinds of bodies in the early Republic and in the third century BCE.

items.label: Well-off plebeians gained power, though equality did not reach everyone
items.explanation: The textbook says the Struggle gave well-off plebeians access to power and did not bring equality to everyone.

items.label: Livy says the Tables were still the source of Roman law in his own day
items.explanation: He claims the laws of the ten tables still stood behind public and private law centuries later.

questions.prompt: A historian lists six things behind Rome's rise in Italy. Which did Rome face, and which did Rome choose to do?

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group

questions.onCorrect: A condition makes the outcome possible, and a policy is a choice, which is why neither alone explains the result.

items.label: Hostile city-states and tribes surrounded Rome
items.explanation: Rome did not choose its neighbours. The textbook names them as the setting in which it expanded.

items.label: Warlike hill tribes east of Latium raided from time to time

items.explanation: The textbook calls this divide and conquer, a method Rome used.

items.label: Rome fought on after defeats until it won a major battle, then negotiated
items.explanation: The textbook calls it negotiating from strength, a way of choosing when to make peace.

items.label: Rome planted colonies on conquered land and linked them by roads
items.explanation: Both were things Rome built, as a first line of defence and to bring armies quickly.

items.label: Rome let beaten peoples keep self-government if they sent troops
items.explanation: It was an offer Rome made, and some of those peoples also received citizenship.

questions.prompt: A modern textbook says Rome made former enemies into loyal allies who governed themselves as long as they honoured Rome's other alliances and sent troops in wartime. questions.prompt: The First Punic War ended in 241 BCE and the Second began in 218 BCE. How many years passed between them?

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two dates. A gap between dates is their difference, because both are counted back from the same point.

questions.prompt: Sallust writes that before Carthage was destroyed, fear of an enemy kept the state in good order. What kind of claim is that?

hints: Could you check the sentence against a document the way you could check a date?

choices.label: A fact
An interpretation
A piece of evidence

questions.prompt: The textbook says that on Delos ten thousand people were 'reportedly' sold in a day. What does 'reportedly' tell a careful reader?

questions.prompt: A historian's notes on Rome after 146 BCE contain six statements. Which kind is each: a fact claim, a piece of evidence, or an interpretation?
hints: Ask whether you could check the statement against a record, or whether it reports what a source says, or whether it explains.

questions.onCorrect: A historian needs all three, and trouble starts when an interpretation is quoted as if it were a fact.

items.label: Carthage and Corinth were destroyed in 146 BCE
items.explanation: It states what happened and when, and it can be checked against other records.

items.label: The war with Jugurtha began in 112 BCE

items.explanation: It reports what a source says, which is material for a historian to examine.

items.label: Once Carthage was gone, fear no longer held the Roman state together
items.explanation: It picks one cause and weighs it, so it is an explanation and not a record.

items.label: Long wars drove small farmers off the land and into the city
items.explanation: It links wars to a social change and gives a cause, which is an explanation.

questions.prompt: Sallust has just said that Marius enlisted whoever was willing, most of them from the lowest ranks. How should a historian record what he goes on to say about why Marius did it?

acceptedIdeas: As two explanations Sallust reports without choosing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As two explanations Sallust reports without choosing

questions.onCorrect: Sallust names who held each view but gives no verdict, and a historian keeps that hedge when summarising him.

extracts.text: Some said that this was done from a scarcity of better men, and others from the consul's desire to pay court to the poorer class, because it was by that order of men that he had been honored and promoted; and, indeed, to a man grasping at power, the most needy are the most serviceable, persons to whom their property (as they have none) is not an object of care, and to whom every thing lucrative appears honorable.
extracts.who: Sallust, Jugurthine War (translated by J. S. Watson)
extracts.when: written around 41 BCE, some forty-five years after Marius died
extracts.kind: A history of the war with Jugurtha, written for Roman readers

choices.label: As two explanations Sallust reports without choosing
As Sallust's own finding that Marius wanted the poor as followers
As the established cause of the change in how armies were raised
As a rumour started by Marius's enemies to discredit him

misconceptions.feedback: Sallust's remark about a man grasping at power says what the needy are useful for, and he attaches it to no one's motive. He sets it among the things said, so it does not settle why Marius acted.

questions.prompt: Sallust gives Marius this speech to the people. What is it best evidence of?
hints: Who wrote the speech down, and how long after Marius spoke?

questions.onCorrect: The speech shows the case Sallust gave Marius, in Sallust's own language, which makes it good evidence of his picture of the man.

extracts.text: Our nobility, relying on their forefathers' merits, though totally different from them in conduct, disparage us who emulate their virtues; and demand of you every public honor, as due, not to their personal merit, but to their high rank. Arrogant pretenders, and utterly unreasonable! For though their ancestors left them all that was at their disposal, their riches, their statues, and their glorious names, they left them not, nor could leave them, their virtue; which alone, of all their possessions, could neither be communicated nor received.
extracts.who: Sallust, Jugurthine War (translated by J. S. Watson)

choices.label: The exact words Marius used when he addressed the people in Rome

How Sallust chose to present Marius's case against the nobility

misconceptions.feedback: Rolfe notes that Sallust's speeches “do not purport to give the exact words of the speakers”, and that their language is Sallust's own. A speech in a history cannot be taken for a transcript.
Only one side speaks here, and it is Marius as Sallust drew him. What the nobles thought would need a source made by them.
A composed speech is still evidence, of Sallust's picture of the man and of the case he thought Marius could make. It is weak only as evidence of the exact words.

questions.prompt: Plutarch reports how Sulla came to be dictator. What does the passage point to, set against the office as it had been before?
hints: What does a gap of 120 years say about how often the office was used?
Which parts of the passage are the old office, and which are new?

acceptedIdeas: Change: an old emergency office revived and held for years
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Change: an old emergency office revived and held for years

questions.onCorrect: The name continued, but an office unused for 120 years, then held for years by one man, marks a change.

extracts.text: For Sylla had declared himself dictator, an office which had then been laid aside for the space of one hundred and twenty years. There was, likewise, an act of grace passed on his behalf, granting indemnity for what was passed, and for the future entrusting him with the power of life and death, confiscation, division of lands, erecting and demolishing of cities, taking away of kingdoms, and bestowing them at pleasure.
extracts.who: Plutarch, Life of Sulla (translated by John Dryden, revised by A. H. Clough)
extracts.when: written by a Greek born about the middle of the first century CE
extracts.kind: A biography written for Greek and Roman readers

choices.label: Continuity: dictators had been appointed regularly until Sulla's time
Change: an old emergency office revived and held for years
Continuity: Sulla held the office exactly as earlier dictators had
Nothing, since a number like 120 years cannot be checked at all

misconceptions.feedback: A gap of 120 years means no one had held the office for generations. Regular use would leave no such gap.
The name was the same, but an office unused for 120 years, revived by a special act that also forgave what Sulla had already done, was not being held in the usual way.
The textbook dates the last use to the Second Punic War, and a count back from Sulla agrees to within a year. A number can be tested against a second account.

questions.prompt: This case is invented. A chronicler and a modern textbook both write about the Duke of Carrow's new army of hired soldiers. Which of these statements report what happened or was said, and which are conclusions drawn later?
hints: Ask of each statement whether the writer could have seen it or been told it, or whether it needs knowledge of what came later.
Words such as led to, ended and turning point belong to a writer who knows the outcome.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The three statements by the chronicler report what happened or was said, and the three by the textbook are conclusions about what it led to.

questions.onCorrect: A conclusion is drawn by someone who knows how things turned out, whether the report under it was firm or hedged.

items.label: The chronicler writes that some said the duke hired foreign soldiers because his barons could not be trusted
items.explanation: It passes on what people said and does not vouch for it, as Sallust does with his two reasons.

items.label: The chronicler writes that the duke paid his soldiers from the tolls of the river bridge
items.explanation: It is a statement about what was done, of a kind a writer of the time could have seen or been told.

items.label: The textbook writes that the duke's hired army ended the barons' hold on the duchy
items.explanation: It names an outcome and its cause together, which only hindsight can do.

items.label: The chronicler writes that on the third day the duke ordered the town gates shut
items.explanation: It tells one thing that happened on one day.

items.label: The textbook writes that hired armies of this kind led to rule by commanders
items.explanation: It generalises from the duke's army to armies of a kind, as the textbook does with client armies.

items.label: The textbook writes that the duke's reform was the turning point between feudal and modern war
items.explanation: A turning point is a judgement about a whole period, made by someone who knows what came after.

questions.prompt: The extract is Sallust's account of why Marius opened the army to the poor. A modern textbook says that Marius's reform opened the army to the poor and led to professional armies of men loyal to their commander. Which statement describes the two best?
hints: Look at the verbs. Does each source say “led to”, or “some said”?
Which one commits itself to a cause, and which one leaves the choice open?

acceptedIdeas: The textbook commits to a result, while the extract leaves the choice open
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The textbook commits to a result, while the extract leaves the choice open

questions.onCorrect: A summary can sound surer than the sources it summarises, which is why a historian asks what each claim rests on.

extracts.text: Some said that this was done from a scarcity of better men, and others from the consul's desire to pay court to the poorer class, because it was by that order of men that he had been honored and promoted
extracts.who: Sallust, Jugurthine War (translated by J. S. Watson)
extracts.when: written around 41 BCE, some forty-five years after Marius died
extracts.kind: A history of the war with Jugurtha, written for Roman readers

choices.label: The extract is the surer, because it gives two reasons and the textbook only one
They agree, since both say that poorer men entered the army
The textbook commits to a result, while the extract leaves the choice open
The textbook is the better source, because it was written more recently

misconceptions.feedback: More reasons do not make a writer surer. The extract offers two without choosing, which shows doubt, and the textbook commits to one result.
They agree about who entered the army. They differ in how sure they are of the cause, which is the point of the question.
Date alone does not rank sources. The textbook is a summary and the extract stands nearer the events, and each has to be read for what it can show.

questions.prompt: Put these five steps in the break between army and state in the order they happened.
hints: Marius's election comes first, and the two marches on Rome fall within two years of each other.
Sulla cannot give up an office before he has taken it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Marius was elected for 107 BCE. Sulla marched on Rome in 88 and Marius in 87, Sulla became dictator in late 82 or early 81, and he resigned in 79.

questions.onCorrect: Both marches on Rome came before the dictatorship, so using an army against the city was already a precedent when Sulla took the office.

items: Marius is elected consul and enlists the poor
Sulla's six legions march on Rome
Marius rallies his veterans and marches on Rome
Sulla takes the dictatorship
Sulla gives the dictatorship up

questions.prompt: Plutarch says Sulla posted names and offered two talents to anyone who killed a man on them. What is the name for such a published list?
hints: The word names the list, not the office Sulla held.
The list let anyone kill the men named on it, and their property was seized.

acceptedIdeas: proscription
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: proscription

questions.onCorrect: Sulla held the dictatorship, and the lists were what he did with it: a public order to kill, with a reward attached.

misconceptions.feedback: The dictatorship is the office Sulla held. The list of names he posted has a name of its own.
A client army is an army loyal to its commander, and a triumvirate an alliance of three men. The list of names is something else.

questions.prompt: Sallust says why he is writing about Catiline. How should a historian treat his statement about his own mind?
hints: Is the sentence a fact about the book, or something Sallust says about himself?
What could you check, outside the sentence, to see whether it is true?

acceptedIdeas: As a claim to be tested against what the book actually does
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As a claim to be tested against what the book actually does

questions.onCorrect: A statement of impartiality is evidence of how the writer wants to be read, and the book and his career are what test it.

extracts.text: as my mind was uninfluenced by hope, fear, or political partisanship. I shall accordingly give a brief account, with as much truth as I can, of the Conspiracy of Catiline
extracts.who: Sallust, Conspiracy of Catiline (translated by J. S. Watson)
extracts.when: written after Caesar's death in 44 BCE, some twenty years after the plot
extracts.kind: A history of the plot, written for Roman readers; the extract begins in the middle of a sentence

choices.label: As proof that the whole book is written without a side
As a sign that Sallust is hiding a bias he knows he has
As a claim to be tested against what the book actually does
As a reason to ignore the book, since all writers take sides

misconceptions.feedback: A writer's statement about himself cannot prove that the book is neutral. It is one more sentence he chose to write, and the book has to be read to see whether it matches.
Nothing in the sentence shows hidden bias. It is a claim, which is neither believed on trust nor thrown out, and a historian checks it against the book and the writer's career.
Having a side limits what a source can show, but it does not make the source useless. The task is to see which parts the side could have shaped.

questions.prompt: In this passage Sallust reports what two of Caesar's enemies did when Cicero would not have Caesar accused. What is the passage best evidence of?
hints: Who does Sallust say spread the stories, and what does he say about their reasons?
Could Sallust know what Caesar did in secret, or only what was said and done in public?

acceptedIdeas: How Sallust presents the stories against Caesar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How Sallust presents the stories against Caesar

questions.onCorrect: Sallust's own wording tells us how he wants the affair seen, which makes the passage evidence of his handling of rumour more than of events.

extracts.text: But when they failed to persuade the consul to such injustice, they themselves, by going from one person to another, and spreading fictions of their own, which they pretended to have heard from Volturcius or the Allobroges, excited such violent odium against him, that certain Roman knights, who were stationed as an armed guard round the Temple of Concord, being prompted, either by the greatness of the danger, or by the impulse of a high spirit, to testify more openly their zeal for the republic, threatened Caesar with their swords as he went out of the senate-house.
extracts.who: Sallust, Conspiracy of Catiline (translated by J. S. Watson)
extracts.when: written after Caesar's death in 44 BCE, some twenty years after the plot
extracts.kind: A history of the plot, written for Roman readers

choices.label: That Caesar took no part in the plot and was wrongly accused
That the stories were true, since armed men acted on them
That Cicero and Caesar were close friends and allies
How Sallust presents the stories against Caesar

misconceptions.feedback: The passage tells us that Caesar's enemies failed to get him accused and then spread stories. That the stories were false is how Sallust presents them, and it cannot show what Caesar did.
Knights who threaten a man with swords show that the stories were believed, which is a different matter from their being true.
The passage says only that Cicero would not have Caesar falsely accused. It gives no sign of friendship between the two.

questions.prompt: Source A is Sallust and Source B is Plutarch. For each statement, who tells it in these two passages?
hints: Read each statement and look for it in Source A, then in Source B.
