acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both put suspicion on Caesar and a decision in Cicero's hands. Only Sallust has the knights and the stories from informers, and only Plutarch has Cato, the decree and Caesar's objection.

questions.onCorrect: The overlap is one point, and the pack does not show whether Plutarch drew on Sallust or on a common source.

extracts.text: But when they failed to persuade the consul to such injustice, they themselves, by going from one person to another, and spreading fictions of their own, which they pretended to have heard from Volturcius or the Allobroges, excited such violent odium against him, that certain Roman knights, who were stationed as an armed guard round the Temple of Concord, being prompted, either by the greatness of the danger, or by the impulse of a high spirit, to testify more openly their zeal for the republic, threatened Caesar with their swords as he went out of the senate-house.
extracts.who: Sallust, Conspiracy of Catiline (translated by J. S. Watson)
extracts.when: written after Caesar's death in 44 BCE, some twenty years after the plot
extracts.kind: A history of the plot, written for Roman readers

extracts.text: Cato followed, and so vehemently urged in his speech the strong suspicion about Caesar himself, and so filled the senate with anger and resolution, that a decree was passed for the execution of the conspirators. But Caesar opposed the confiscation of their goods, not thinking it fair that those who had rejected the mildest part of his sentence should avail themselves of the severest. And when many insisted upon it, he appealed to the tribunes, but they would do nothing; till Cicero himself yielding, remitted that part of the sentence.
extracts.who: Plutarch, Life of Cicero (translated by John Dryden, revised by A. H. Clough)
extracts.when: written by a Greek born about the middle of the first century CE
extracts.kind: A biography written for Greek and Roman readers

items.label: Suspicion fell on Caesar during the affair
items.explanation: Sallust has Caesar's enemies spread stories about him, and Plutarch has Cato raise strong suspicion of him.

items.label: Cicero made a decision that touched Caesar
items.explanation: In Sallust he refuses to have Caesar falsely accused, and in Plutarch he gives way over the confiscation that Caesar opposed.

items.label: Armed knights threatened Caesar as he left the senate-house
items.explanation: Only Sallust's passage has the knights and their swords.

items.label: Caesar's enemies spread stories they claimed to have heard from informers
items.explanation: Only Sallust names the stories and their source.

items.label: Cato's speech filled the Senate with anger and led to a decree for the executions
items.explanation: Only Plutarch's passage reports Cato's speech and the decree.

items.explanation: Only Plutarch's passage has Caesar's objection and the appeal.

questions.prompt: The first triumvirate was made in 60 BCE and Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE. By the year numbers, how many years is that?
hints: Years BCE count down, so 49 BCE is the later year.
Take the later year's number away from the earlier year's.
Count from 60 down to 49 and check whether your count includes both end years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Years BCE count down, so the difference is 60 minus 49, which is 11 years.

questions.onCorrect: Eleven years of alliance, command in Gaul and a death passed before the war, and a cause claim has to cover them.

misconceptions.feedback: 10 leaves out an end year. Take the two year numbers and find the difference between them again.
12 counts both end years as whole years. Subtract the two year numbers instead of counting them.

questions.prompt: Plutarch says the civil wars began from the union of Pompey, Crassus and Caesar and not from their later quarrel. What would most strengthen that claim?
hints: A claim about a cause is strong when it explains something that came before the effect.
What would the union have had to change, years before the war, for it to count as the origin?

acceptedIdeas: Evidence of what the alliance did to the Senate before the quarrel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Evidence of what the alliance did to the Senate before the quarrel

questions.onCorrect: A cause claim gains strength from changes the cause made before the effect, and not from repetition or from the effect itself.

choices.label: A later writer repeating the sentence in almost the same words
Evidence that Pompey and Caesar did later fall out with each other
Evidence of what the alliance did to the Senate before the quarrel
Evidence that most men at the time blamed the quarrel for the war

misconceptions.feedback: A repeat adds nothing if it was copied from Plutarch. Support needs a second source that did not get the claim from the first.
Plutarch accepts the quarrel. The claim is about which came first as the origin, and the quarrel's existence does not choose between the two.
Plutarch already says most men think so. What most people believed does not show whether they were right.

questions.prompt: Source A is a rule from the Twelve Tables and Source B an accusation recorded by Plutarch. What do the two together show about the charge against Cicero?
hints: What does Source A say Rome's rule was, and what does Source B say Cicero was charged with?
Does either passage say whether the charge was upheld?

acceptedIdeas: The charge appealed to an old rule, but neither passage decides it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The charge appealed to an old rule, but neither passage decides it

questions.onCorrect: A law and an accusation show what Cicero's critics pointed to, and neither shows how the case ended.

extracts.text: Putting to death of any man, whosoever he might be unconvicted is forbidden.
extracts.who: Twelve Tables, Table IX, clause 6 (translated by O. J. Thatcher, 1901, modernised by J. S. Arkenberg)
extracts.when: traditionally dated to about 450 BCE
extracts.kind: Rome's first written laws

extracts.text: At which Caesar being exasperated, joined the party of Clodius against him, and wholly alienated Pompey from him; he also himself declared in a public assembly of the people, that he did not think Lentulus and Cethegus, with their accomplices, were fairly and legally put to death without being brought to trial. And this, indeed, was the crime charged upon Cicero, and this impeachment he was summoned to answer.
extracts.who: Plutarch, Life of Cicero (translated by John Dryden, revised by A. H. Clough)
extracts.when: written by a Greek born about the middle of the first century CE
extracts.kind: A biography written for Greek and Roman readers

choices.label: The charge appealed to an old rule, but neither passage decides it
That the executions broke Table IX and so Cicero was clearly guilty
That Plutarch invented the charge, since Table IX is far too early
That the Twelve Tables were the only written law Rome had in 63 BCE

misconceptions.feedback: Source B reports a charge and Caesar's view, not a verdict. Charging a man with breaking a rule does not show that he did.
Table IX is traditionally dated to about 450 BCE, which makes it earlier, not inapplicable. Plutarch reports the charge as one actually brought.
Neither passage says anything about other laws. A rule being old does not make it the only one.

questions.prompt: A town clerk, in an invented case, writes at the head of the minutes that he has taken no side in a dispute, and a rival's letter says he lent money to the winner. What does the lesson call the clerk's statement?
hints: The clerk is saying something about himself. What is it that he says?
The lesson names a writer's statement that he has no interest in the matter.

acceptedIdeas: claimed impartiality
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: claimed impartiality

questions.onCorrect: The statement is a claim the clerk chose to write, and the rival's letter is the kind of outside evidence that tests it.

misconceptions.feedback: Bias is what the rival's letter suggests. The term asked for names the clerk's own statement that he has none.
Corroboration is support from a second source. The clerk's statement is a claim about himself, and the letter is the test of it.

questions.prompt: Put these five steps on the road to the Rubicon in the order they happened.
hints: The alliance came first, and the consulship came the year after it.
Caesar could not cross the Rubicon until he had been in Gaul for years.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The triumvirate was formed in 60 BCE, Caesar was consul in 59, his campaigns in Gaul began in 58, Crassus was killed at Carrhae in 53 and Caesar crossed the Rubicon in January 49.

questions.onCorrect: The alliance was eleven years old, and Crassus was already dead, when Caesar crossed the Rubicon.

Caesar holds the consulship
Caesar's campaigns in Gaul begin

Caesar crosses the Rubicon

questions.prompt: Caesar says why he marched into Gaul in 58 BCE. Who is that explanation written for?
hints: Who could read a book in Rome in Caesar's lifetime, and who would decide whether his war was proper?
Is a reason for starting a war a plain record, or something meant to win agreement?

acceptedIdeas: Readers at Rome who would judge whether the war was justified
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Readers at Rome who would judge whether the war was justified

questions.onCorrect: Edwards suggests that the Gallic War would have served as a vindication of Caesar's campaigns to the Senate, which is what a justification is for.

extracts.text: If this took place, he saw that it would be attended with great danger to the Province to have warlike men, enemies of the Roman people, bordering upon an open and very fertile tract of country.

extracts.when: about the campaign of 58 BCE, perhaps published in 51 BCE
extracts.kind: A commentary: the general's own report of his campaigns, written for readers at Rome

choices.label: Soldiers in his camp who needed to be told why they were marching
Readers at Rome who would judge whether the war was justified
Historians writing centuries later who would want the facts
Nobody in particular, since a report only records what happened

misconceptions.feedback: A commentary is a book, and its readers were people who could read it in Rome. The reason is addressed to them, and the soldiers had no need of a book.
Caesar was writing for his own time, and he chose his reasons with his own readers' judgement in mind.
A general's report of his own war is written by a party to it, and a reason given for starting a war is meant to persuade.

questions.prompt: Caesar's lists, found in the Helvetian camp, give 368,000 as the number who set out, and the extract follows them. By his figures, how many of those who set out were not counted among the people who returned home?
hints: Which two figures does the question ask you to compare: those who set out, and those counted at home?
The figure for those who could bear arms is a different group and is not needed.
Take away the number counted at home from the number who set out.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 368,000 set out and 110,000 were counted at home, so 368,000 minus 110,000 is 258,000 not counted at home.

questions.onCorrect: The 258,000 is our subtraction, not Caesar's statement, and the census it rests on was taken at his order and reported by him.

extracts.text: Out of these, such as could bear arms [amounted] to about 92,000. When the census of those who returned home was taken, as Caesar had commanded, the number was found to be 110,000.
extracts.who: Caesar, Gallic War, book 1 (translated by W. A. McDevitte and W. S. Bohn)
extracts.when: about the campaign of 58 BCE, perhaps published in 51 BCE
extracts.kind: A commentary: the general's own report, here of lists found in an enemy camp

276,000 takes away the 92,000 who could bear arms. The number counted at home is a different figure.

questions.prompt: The five groups add up to the total that Caesar gives. What does that show?

That Caesar did not change any of the figures he reports
That the lists agree with themselves, and nothing more
That the census of those who went home must also be right

misconceptions.feedback: A list can add up and still be wrong about the people in it. The sum checks the arithmetic, and the counting is a separate matter.
The sum would be the same if a writer had altered the figures consistently. It does not tell us what happened between the lists and Caesar's page.
The census is a different count, made later at Caesar's order. The sum of the five lists says nothing about it.

questions.prompt: Caesar reports what he told his soldiers at the start of the civil war. What is the passage best evidence of?

extracts.when: about the war that began in 49 BCE, left unfinished at his death in 44 BCE
extracts.kind: A commentary: Caesar's own summary of what he told his soldiers, in the third person

extracts.text: When he came to the river Rubicon, which parts Gaul within the Alps from the rest of Italy, his thoughts began to work, now he was just entering upon the danger, and he wavered much in his mind, when he considered the greatness of the enterprise into which he was throwing himself.
extracts.who: Plutarch, Life of Caesar (translated by John Dryden, revised by A. H. Clough)
extracts.when: written by a Greek born about the middle of the first century CE
extracts.kind: A biography written for Greek and Roman readers

choices.label: Source A is accurate and Source B is invented to make a good story
Source A is Caesar's case for acting, Source B a later writer's picture
Source B contradicts Source A about what Caesar did when war began
Both are eyewitness accounts of the very same moment in the war

misconceptions.feedback: Neither label follows from the passages. Source A is Caesar's own case and Source B a later writer's scene, and each has to be tested before it is trusted.
They describe different moments, a speech to soldiers and a halt at a river, and neither denies the other.
Source A is Caesar's own report of a speech and Source B is Plutarch's scene, written long after. They are not accounts of one moment.

questions.prompt: Put these five events of Caesar's career in the order they happened.
hints: The war in Gaul began before any of the civil war.
Pharsalus was fought in the war that the Rubicon began.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Helvetian campaign began in 58 BCE, Crassus was killed in 53, Caesar crossed the Rubicon in January 49, won at Pharsalus in 48 and was assassinated in 44.

questions.onCorrect: Caesar's own books cover the first of these events and the war that began with the third; Plutarch wrote of all five long after.

items: Caesar's campaign against the Helvetii begins
Crassus is killed fighting the Parthians
Caesar crosses the Rubicon
Caesar defeats Pompey at Pharsalus
Caesar is assassinated

questions.prompt: A modern article states that 368,000 Helvetii and their allies set out, as though it were established fact. What is the best reason to treat the figure as a claim?
hints: Who found the lists, and who tells us what was on them?
Is there a second report of the lists that did not come from Caesar?

acceptedIdeas: Caesar alone reports the lists, so nothing else checks them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Caesar alone reports the lists, so nothing else checks them

questions.onCorrect: A figure that reaches us through one man needs a second route to the event before a historian treats it as fact.

choices.label: Ancient writers were unable to count so many people reliably
Plutarch gives a quite different total for the Gallic wars
The five groups do not add up to the total Caesar reports
Caesar alone reports the lists, so nothing else checks them

misconceptions.feedback: Ancient lists of large numbers can be reliable or not. The reason to hesitate is where this one comes from, and not the size of the figure.
Plutarch's totals count the whole of the Gallic wars and not this migration, so they neither confirm nor contradict the figure.
They do add up, to 368,000. Agreement of the arithmetic is not the weakness here.

questions.prompt: The Res Gestae was set up in public, and it speaks in the first person. What does that suggest about how to read this opening claim?
hints: Who is speaking in the passage, and who is meant to read it?
Does being displayed in public make a text more neutral, or more careful about its image?

acceptedIdeas: As a statement meant to shape how he was remembered
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As a statement meant to shape how he was remembered

questions.onCorrect: A text set up in public shows how its author wanted to be seen. What it says still has to be tested.

extracts.text: At the age of nineteen, on my own initiative and at my own expense, I raised an army by means of which I restored liberty to the republic, which had been oppressed by the tyranny of a faction.
extracts.who: Augustus, Res Gestae (translated by F. W. Shipley, Loeb, 1924)
extracts.when: begun well before 14 CE, the year he died, and copied on temple walls
extracts.kind: His own list of his deeds, displayed in public

choices.label: As a private record of what Augustus really thought
As a statement meant to shape how he was remembered
As a list that any reader could check against the record
As a neutral summary prepared by officials

misconceptions.feedback: A text cut in stone and copied on temple walls is public, and a private record would not be.
Display shows that the author cared how the text was seen. It does not show that readers could test it.
The text speaks as “I”, so it is Augustus speaking, with the interest in his own memory that goes with that.

questions.prompt: Source A is Augustus on the men who killed Julius Caesar, and Source B is Plutarch on what the three men did together. The Res Gestae mentions neither a list nor Cicero. What does the difference show?
hints: Does a list of a man's own achievements claim to hold everything that happened?
What does the rule about silences, from the History course, say about gaps like this one?

acceptedIdeas: The account is selective, so its silence is a cue to look further
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The account is selective, so its silence is a cue to look further

questions.onCorrect: The silence does not prove the list happened, and it does not prove it did not. It marks a point to check against another source.

extracts.text: Those who slew my father I drove into exile, punishing their deed by due process of law, and afterwards when they waged war upon the republic I twice defeated them in battle.
extracts.who: Augustus, Res Gestae (translated by F. W. Shipley, Loeb, 1924)
extracts.when: begun well before 14 CE, the year he died, and copied on temple walls
extracts.kind: His own list of his deeds, displayed in public

extracts.text: Thus united, they made a schedule of above two hundred persons who were to be put to death. But the greatest contention in all their debates was on the question of Cicero's case.
extracts.who: Plutarch, Life of Cicero (translated by John Dryden, revised by A. H. Clough)
extracts.when: written by a Greek born about the middle of the first century CE
extracts.kind: A biography written for Greek and Roman readers

choices.label: The account is selective, so its silence is a cue to look further
Plutarch invented the list, since Augustus never mentions it at all
Both are complete accounts, and they just disagree with each other
Augustus lied about his career, because he left something out of it

misconceptions.feedback: A silence in a self-account does not show that something never happened. The list is a selective one by design, and Plutarch's report needs a test of its own.
The Res Gestae does not claim to be complete, and Shipley notes that it leaves out whatever is personal. The two are not rival complete accounts.
Leaving something out is not a lie. A selective account can be accurate in what it says and still say nothing where its author would rather not speak.

questions.prompt: Augustus says in the extract that he did not accept the dictatorship. A modern textbook says that in 27 BCE Octavian formally stepped down as dictator. They disagree about the dictatorship. What is the best next step?
hints: Can both statements be true at once?
What would let you decide between a primary source with a motive and a summary with no source?

acceptedIdeas: Look for a third source on whether he ever held the office
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Look for a third source on whether he ever held the office

questions.onCorrect: A conflict between a self-account and a summary is settled by a third source, and neither side wins by being older or newer.

extracts.text: The dictatorship offered me by the people and the Roman Senate, in my absence and later when present, in the consulship of Marcus Marcellus and Lucius Arruntius I did not accept.
extracts.who: Augustus, Res Gestae (translated by F. W. Shipley, Loeb, 1924)
extracts.when: begun well before 14 CE, the year he died, and copied on temple walls
extracts.kind: His own list of his deeds, displayed in public

choices.label: Believe Augustus, since a man knows which offices he held
Believe the textbook, since Augustus had a motive to say he refused
Look for a third source on whether he ever held the office
Treat both as true, since each gives a different year

misconceptions.feedback: A man knows his own career, but he also chooses what to put on a public monument. His knowledge is a reason to take him seriously and not a reason to stop checking.
A motive is a reason to test Augustus's claim. It is not a reason to prefer a sentence that cites nothing, and the textbook has to be tested as well.
They cannot both be true. A man cannot step down from an office that he never accepted.

questions.prompt: Why does the step from 1 BCE to 1 CE add one year and not none?
hints: Which year comes straight after 1 BCE in the way we count?
Is there a year numbered 0 between 1 BCE and 1 CE?

acceptedIdeas: Because 1 CE comes straight after 1 BCE, with no year 0
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because 1 CE comes straight after 1 BCE, with no year 0

questions.onCorrect: With no year 0, the year after 1 BCE is 1 CE, so crossing the boundary adds one year to the two counts.

choices.label: Because 1 CE comes straight after 1 BCE, with no year 0
Because the year 1 CE is counted as one of the BCE years
Because a year 0 lies between the two and counts as a year
Because the calendar itself was changed at the start of 1 CE

misconceptions.feedback: The two eras are separate counts. Years BCE run down to 1 BCE, and years CE start again at 1 CE.
There was no year 0 in this system of dating. 1 CE follows 1 BCE directly.
The numbering is a later convention, and it was not a change in the length of a year. It gives 1 CE as the year after 1 BCE.

questions.prompt: Augustus held tribunician power from 23 BCE and died in 14 CE. How many years is that?
hints: 23 BCE is before the boundary between the eras and 14 CE is after it.
Add the two year numbers, since one lies on each side of the boundary.
There is no year 0, so take one year off the sum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Across the boundary the years are added and one is taken away, so 23 + 14 - 1 = 36 years.

questions.onCorrect: Across the BCE and CE boundary the years are added and one is taken away, since there is no year 0.

misconceptions.feedback: 37 is the sum with no year taken off. Counting 23 BCE as the first year gives 37 as the number of the last year, which is a different question.
9 takes 14 from 23, as if both years were BCE. A year CE lies on the other side of the boundary.

questions.prompt: After 27 BCE the consuls and the Senate still met, but Augustus held tribunician power and command of the frontier armies. How is that best described?
hints: Which things in the question continued, and which did Augustus add?
Does an office keep its old power just because it keeps its old name?

acceptedIdeas: Offices continued while, says the textbook, power moved to one man
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Offices continued while, says the textbook, power moved to one man

questions.onCorrect: The principate kept the old offices and added one man's hold on them, which is why the textbook calls the Republic a façade.

choices.label: The Republic returned unchanged, exactly as Augustus says it did
Every old office was abolished and replaced by offices of his own
Offices continued while, says the textbook, power moved to one man
Nothing changed at all, because the same offices existed as before

misconceptions.feedback: Augustus says he handed the republic back, but the textbook says he held a tribune's powers and command of the army together. It calls the result a façade.
Consuls, the Senate and the assemblies still met, and Augustus himself held the consulship. What changed, on the textbook's account, was who held the power.
The offices existed, but the textbook says one man now held the powers of a tribune and command of the army, and a historian has to count that as change.

questions.prompt: Augustus says this about the years after he handed the republic back. Which evidence would best test the claim about power?
hints: The claim is about power and not about rank. What kind of evidence shows what a man could do?
Which of these options come from outside Augustus's own text?

acceptedIdeas: A record of the powers the Senate voted him in 27 and 23 BCE
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A record of the powers the Senate voted him in 27 and 23 BCE

questions.onCorrect: Power is tested by what a man could do, which the Senate's grants and the textbook's account record, and not by titles or copies.

extracts.text: After that time I took precedence of all in rank, but of power I possessed no more than those who were my colleagues in any magistracy.
extracts.who: Augustus, Res Gestae (translated by F. W. Shipley, Loeb, 1924)
extracts.when: begun well before 14 CE, the year he died, and copied on temple walls
extracts.kind: His own list of his deeds, displayed in public

choices.label: A longer list of the honours and titles that he was given
Another copy of the Res Gestae cut on a different temple wall
The exact date on which the Res Gestae was cut in stone
A record of the powers the Senate voted him in 27 and 23 BCE

misconceptions.feedback: Titles and honours show rank, which Augustus admits when he says he took precedence of all. The claim is about power, so it needs evidence of what he could do.
Copies of the same text repeat his claim and do not test it.
A date for the inscription says when the claim was published, not whether it was true.

questions.prompt: Put these six steps from Caesar's death to the powers of 23 BCE in the order they happened.
hints: Brutus and Cassius were Caesar's killers, and the triumvirate was formed to deal with them.
The title Augustus and the tribunician powers both came after Actium.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Caesar was killed in 44 BCE, the second triumvirate was formed in 43, Philippi was fought in 42, Actium in 31, the title Augustus came in 27 and the tribunician powers in 23.

questions.onCorrect: The powers that the textbook sets at the centre of the settlement came last, twenty-one years after Caesar's death.

items: Julius Caesar is assassinated
Octavian, Antony and Lepidus form the second triumvirate
Brutus and Cassius are defeated at Philippi
Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra at Actium
The Senate gives Octavian the title Augustus
The Senate gives Augustus the powers of a tribune

questions.prompt: A historian says that a town kept its council and its elections, but that one family now decided everything. What term does the lesson use for an outward form kept after the substance has changed?
hints: The council and the elections are the outward form. What is the word for such a form with nothing behind it?
The textbook uses the word of Augustus's Republic.

acceptedIdeas: facade
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: facade

questions.onCorrect: A facade keeps the outward form of an institution and says nothing about who holds the power behind it.

misconceptions.feedback: The principate is the name of Augustus's system, in which a first citizen held power through the old offices. The word asked for names the outward form kept after the substance has changed.
A tradition is a story or practice handed down. The word asked for names an outward form that is kept while the substance changes.

flashcards.front: In which year BCE does Roman tradition place the founding of Rome?
flashcards.back: 753 BCE, by Roman tradition: nobody recorded the founding when it happened.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 753 BCE, by Roman tradition: nobody recorded the founding when it happened.

flashcards.front: What is the word for a story told to show conduct a reader should copy or avoid?
flashcards.back: An exemplum: Livy tells much of the early city's story this way.

acceptedIdeas: exemplum
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: exemplum

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why is the Lucretia scene still evidence although it cannot show what happened in 509 BCE?
flashcards.back: It shows how a Roman writer of Livy's day told the end of the kings and what he thought a reader should admire.

flashcards.front: What is the word for a tribune's power to stop an act by saying 'I forbid'?
flashcards.back: A veto: used by a tribune, it could stop the Senate from passing a decree or even meeting.

acceptedIdeas: veto
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: veto

flashcards.front: Which body controlled the treasury in Polybius's account?
flashcards.back: The Senate: the quaestors could not issue public money without its decree, except for the consuls' service.

acceptedIdeas: Senate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Senate

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why should a reader check Polybius's picture of a balanced constitution against another source?
flashcards.back: He is a Greek explaining why Rome won, so he has a reason to find the system well balanced.

flashcards.front: About when are the Twelve Tables traditionally dated (year BCE)?
flashcards.back: About 450 BCE: Rome's first written laws, published in the Forum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About 450 BCE: Rome's first written laws, published in the Forum.

flashcards.front: What do we call a refusal by the plebeians to serve or to stay in the city until their demands were met?
flashcards.back: A secession, as in Livy's story of the withdrawal to the sacred mount.

acceptedIdeas: secession
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: secession

flashcards.front: In a sentence, what is a law like Table III evidence of, and what can it not show?
flashcards.back: It shows what lawmakers meant to allow or forbid, and it cannot show how often anyone acted on it.

flashcards.front: What is the word for a self-governing Italian community tied to Rome by treaty, which sent troops when the consuls asked?
flashcards.back: An ally: it kept its own government in return for troops and loyalty to Rome's other alliances.

acceptedIdeas: ally
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ally

flashcards.front: How many men are in four legions of 4,200 infantry and 300 horse each?
flashcards.back: 18,000: 4,500 men in a legion, times four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 18,000: 4,500 men in a legion, times four.

flashcards.front: In a sentence, how do a condition and a policy differ in explaining Rome's rise in Italy?
flashcards.back: A condition is what Rome faced, such as hostile neighbours, and a policy is what Rome chose to do, such as planting colonies.

flashcards.front: Livy begins the oath of Hannibal with 'There is besides a story'. What kind of claim is it?
flashcards.back: A hedged report: Livy passes it on without vouching for it.

acceptedIdeas: hedged report
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: hedged report

flashcards.front: When historians sort what lies behind a war, what three kinds of factor do they distinguish?
flashcards.back: Conditions are long-standing background, a cause pushes events along, and a trigger is the event that sets them off.

flashcards.front: The First Punic War ended in 241 BCE and the Second began in 218 BCE. How many years between them?
flashcards.back: The gap is 241 minus 218, which is 23 years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The gap is 241 minus 218, which is 23 years.

flashcards.front: In this translation of Livy, 40,000 foot and 2,700 horse 'are said to have been slain' at Cannae. What is the total, in men?
flashcards.back: The total is 42,700 in this translation, and 'are said to have been' shows Livy cannot vouch for it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 42,700 in this translation, and 'are said to have been' shows Livy cannot vouch for it.

flashcards.front: What do we call the earlier writer that a historian names as the source of a claim?
flashcards.back: An authority: it lets a reader follow the claim back, as Livy follows Fabius.

acceptedIdeas: authority
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: authority

flashcards.front: Say how you would weigh Polybius against the textbook on Rome's allies after Cannae.
flashcards.back: Ask what each means by 'allies' and which moment it describes before deciding which to trust.

flashcards.front: What do we call an explanation of events by the habits and character of a people or its leaders?
flashcards.back: A moral explanation, such as Sallust's claim that fear of Carthage kept Rome in order.

acceptedIdeas: moral explanation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: moral explanation

flashcards.front: Carthage fell in 146 BCE and the war with Jugurtha began in 112 BCE. How many years between them?
flashcards.back: The gap is 146 minus 112, which is 34 years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The gap is 146 minus 112, which is 34 years.

flashcards.front: Rate how well you could say, for Polybius, Sallust and the textbook, what each thinks went wrong with Rome and what evidence each offers.
flashcards.back: Polybius forecasts that wealth and rivalry for office lead to mob-rule, Sallust blames the loss of fear of Carthage, and the textbook points to wars, lost farms and landless city poor.

flashcards.front: What do we call an official elected by the plebeians who could propose laws and stop the acts of others?
flashcards.back: A tribune, the office Tiberius Gracchus held when he proposed his land law in 133 BCE.

acceptedIdeas: tribune
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: tribune

flashcards.front: Tiberius's law is dated to 133 BCE and Gaius died in 121 BCE. How many years is that?
flashcards.back: The gap is 133 minus 121, which is 12 years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The gap is 133 minus 121, which is 12 years.

flashcards.front: Rate your recall: name the questions to ask of a later account and say which of them the Plutarch passages answer.
flashcards.back: Ask who is named, who is not, what could be checked and what the writer wants; Plutarch names Gaius's writing for one claim and names no one for others.

flashcards.front: What do we call an army whose soldiers are more loyal to their commander, who promises them war gains and land, than to the state?
flashcards.back: A client army, the textbook's name for the armies that followed Marius and Sulla.

acceptedIdeas: client army
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: client army

flashcards.front: According to Plutarch, for how many years had the office of dictator been laid aside before Sulla took it?
flashcards.back: 120 years, which fits the textbook's date for the last dictator, in the Second Punic War.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 120 years, which fits the textbook's date for the last dictator, in the Second Punic War.

flashcards.front: Explain in a sentence why the speech Sallust gives Marius is evidence of Sallust's picture of Marius and not a record of his words.
flashcards.back: Sallust composed the speech, in his own language, so it shows how he saw Marius's case and cannot be trusted for the words spoken.

flashcards.front: What do we call a writer's own statement that he has no interest in the matter he writes about?
flashcards.back: A claimed impartiality, which a historian tests against the writer's career and what his book does.

acceptedIdeas: claimed impartiality
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: claimed impartiality

flashcards.front: What do we call a private alliance of three men, such as the one that joined Pompey, Crassus and Caesar in 60 BCE?
flashcards.back: A triumvirate, here the first, which Plutarch says was the origin of the civil wars.

acceptedIdeas: triumvirate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: triumvirate

flashcards.front: Explain in a sentence why two accounts that agree do not always corroborate each other.
flashcards.back: Corroboration needs a second source that did not get the claim from the first, so two accounts count as one if the later writer copied the earlier.

flashcards.front: What do we call Caesar's own report of his campaigns, written in the third person for readers at Rome?
flashcards.back: A commentary, which is the general's own account and the one he most wanted believed.

acceptedIdeas: commentary
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: commentary

flashcards.front: Caesar's lists give 368,000 who set out. How many does his census count at home?
flashcards.back: 110,000, a census taken at Caesar's command and reported only by him.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 110,000, a census taken at Caesar's command and reported only by him.

flashcards.front: Say in a sentence where the Rubicon scene comes from and what Plutarch says about his source.
flashcards.back: It comes from Plutarch, because Caesar's Book 1 never names the river; Plutarch names Pollio among those present but does not say Pollio was his source.

flashcards.front: What do we call an outward form that is kept after the substance has changed?
flashcards.back: A facade, which is what the textbook says the restored Republic was.

acceptedIdeas: facade
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: facade

flashcards.front: What is the name of Augustus's own list of what he had done, set up in public?
flashcards.back: The Res Gestae, which survives in a copy from a temple at Ancyra.

acceptedIdeas: Res Gestae
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Res Gestae

flashcards.front: Name a claim in the Res Gestae that you tested, the source you tested it against, and what you found.
flashcards.back: For example: Augustus's silence about the lists, tested against Plutarch, found a gap to check and not proof; or his refusal of the dictatorship, set against the textbook, found a conflict that needs a third source.
